speechtext:
'*SETTLEMENT OF DIFFERENCES CONCERNING INDIAN LANDS.
The House resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 13-Hon. Mr. .Meighen- to provide for the settlement of differences between the Governments of the Dominion of Canada and the Province of British Columbia -respecting Indian lands and certain other Indian affairs in the said province, Mr. Boivin in the chair.

On section 2-Power given to Governor in Council to settle differences between Canada and British Columbia respecting Indian matters.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When this Bill was
last in Committee we had reached clause 2, which had been allowed to stand.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The member
for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) is specially interested in this Bill, and I suggest that the Minister of the Interior agree to either a postponement of its consideration, or the taking up of the third reading on a subsequent occasion when the member for Three Rivers is here.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will agree to the second proposal.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 2 carry?
Read the clause.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The clause was read
when the Bill was last undeir consideration in committee.

When does the minister
expect a final adjustment to l}e arrived at as outlined in clause 2 ? A lot of money has been spent.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As soon as we can get the British Columbia Government to agree. We know our mind in the matter and have communicated with the British Columbia Government accordingly. We have not been able to get their acquiescence, nor have we been able to get as yet a definite statement of their position in the premises. We intend to address ourselves to a solution just as soon as .we have the power to do so.
How much additional cost will be involved?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: None at all. The expenditure was all made long before I took over the department.

The minister
stated the other day, when we were discussing the Bill, that the report had been made some time ago. I should like to know if the report is printed and available to the members.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I could not say definitely as to the report being printed, although I am morally certain that it was printed. But I know it is available to members; it was laid on the Table of the House some years ago and may now be found in the hands of the proper custodian.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.

On section 3-power to order reductions or cut-offs from Reserves without surrender by Indians.

Possibly it is my fault that I do not know very much about this subject, but perhaps the minister would not mind giving us some explanation as to the extent of land that is dealt with in this Bill and what is included in the purport of this legislation. Although we might have had an opportunity of seeing this report, we did not see it, and the minister might, therefore, give us a brief explanation of the report.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The report, as the hon. member knows, is the report of a joint commission appointed by the Government of British Columbia and the Government of the Dominion of Canada pursuant to Orders in Council passed by the respective Governments, embodying an agreement entered into by Sir Richard McBride and representatives of the Indian Department. The agreement provided for the final settlement of differences that had arisen during a period of two or three decades, having to do primarily with the claim of the province of British Columbia to a reversionary interest in all Indian lands in that province, and to a definition of what reversionary interest, if any such exist, should be, and having to do as well with the areas of Indian Reserves in the province, their sufficiency for the purpose of the various tribes or their superabundance in area for the purposes of the tribes. The commission performed its work extending over a very long period of time and made tertain recommendations as to the disposal of the [DOT]question of reversionary interest, as to delimiting Reserves that were believed to be larger than necessary and as to increasing others that were believed to be smaller than essential. The provision of the report covering the subject of reversionary interest aimed at deciding the question in this way, that where land was to be sold that had already been alloted to Indian tribes in Reserves, the proceeds should be divided equally between the province and the Dominion, the Dominion to utilize its moiety in trust for the purpose of the administration	of	the	affairs of the
Indians themselves, the province to be entitled absolutely to its share. The Dominion has not, and indeed the government of the Dominion as a Government would not have constitutional power to admit the existence of a reversionary interest at all; but the terms of
section 13 of the Act of Union and of subsequent Orders that were passed were such that a claim was put forward to this reversionary interest, the same to take effect upon the giving up of any Reserve by the tribe. If a Reserve is given up by a tribe permanently and a new Reserve has to be found, it is essential for the purposes of Indian administration that the proceeds of the sale of the first Reserve should be placed in the trust fund, the same as in the case of all surrenders in the province, for the administration of the affairs of the tribe. The report, as I have pointed out, looks to a settlement of the reversionary interest claim along the lines indicated, and looks to a readjustment of the areas of the various Reserves by means of cutoffs and additions, the amounts being specifically set out in the report. I can give the committee the details as to the amount to be cut off in any special Reserve or as to the amount to be added; the cut-offs exceeded the additions. The principle difficulty involved is in connection with this Kitsilano Reserve in British Columbia. As the hon. member will remember, the Kitsilano Reserve has been taken by the Harbour Commissioners of British Columbia; settlement has not yet been made; but if pursuant to the passing of this Bill we are able to agree upon a settlement in acceptance of the terms of the commission's report, then we shall be able to get the moneys paid by the Harbour Commissioners for the Kitsilano Reserve and to distribute it in pursuance of the terms of the report.
The British Columbia Government has never indicated a willingness to accept the terms of the commission's report. The Orders in Council establishing the commission did not bind either government definitely and absolutely to an acceptance of the report; they bound the governments only to a sympathetic reception of the report and to acquiescence therein to the utmost extent that could be deemed reasonable by each. As a matter of finality that agreement amounted to very little. We have stated our willingness to accept the report in toto; the British Columbia Government made certain tentative suggestions which they afterwards recalled; but they have never placed us in definite and final possession of their views or their position in the premises at all. They, however, obtained from their legislature at its last session, powers to negotiate with the Dominion Government looking to such further adjustments as they think right and to settle with

the Dominion Government finally upon the terms of the report as so adjusted. We are seeking similar powers, and if this Bill passes, we shall have them. It will be obvious to the committee that there would be no use in the Dominion Government taking power to settle the terms of the report, and to agree W'ith the Provincial Government thereon, if it were still in the power of an Indian tribe to refuse acquiescence to any single feature of the report. Consequently, in this clause we ask that we be given power to make such cut-offs- there is no need to do so in respect to the additions-as are essential to the carrying out of the report as it may be jointly amended, if it may be at all, by the two governments. That is the whole purport of this legislation.

I do not doubt that all the objects of this Bill are good, but I cannot help thinking that the clause under consideration is unusually broad. Possibly it has a broader effect than my hon. friend intended. It provides that notwithstanding anything in the Indian Act, the Governor in -Council may make agreements to carry out this purpose. That is a very broad statement. You set aside the whole Indian Act and transfer all its powers as regards this transaction to the Governor in Council. That is giving a good deal of power to the Governor in Council, ani :<t seems to me that if it be intended to depart from the Indian Act, the minister should bring down an amendment to that Act dealing with the case. The clause further provides that the Government:
-may carry on such further negotiations and enter into such further agreements with the Government of the province of British Columbia as may be found necessary for a full and final adjustment of the differences between the said Governments.
These adjustments may involve the payment of money. I do not know whether my hon. friend would contend that under that clause the Governor in Council would have the right to pay -money. However, my main purpose in -calling attention -to this is to point out that the Governor in Council are taking to themselves a very, very broad power. I do not question that it is a good one; I am quite satisfied -that it is all intended for a good end, but I would ask my hon. friend if he thinks it wise to give power to the Governor in Council to set aside absolutely the Indian Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think the clause has the scope the hon. member fears. The

negativing of the Indian Act applies -only to the extent of not requiring surrenders from the Indian tribes themselves. Clause 3 reads -as follows:
For the purpose of adjusting, readjusting or confirming the reductions or cut-offs from reserves in accordance with the recommendations of the Royal Commission, the Governor in Council may order such reductions or cut-offs to be effected without surrenders of the same by the Indians, notwithstanding any provisions of the Indian Act to the contrary.
It is only to that extent that the provisions of the Indian Act are affected at all. We can only negative the Indian Act to the extent that it always required surrenders. The hon. member will see that surrenders by the Indians -are essential before the Indians are substantially affected, or before they can be removed from their reserves, but if surrenders by the Indians are to be required in the case of every little cut-off that is essential here and there, the whole object of the negotiations may be frustrated by the -caprice of one tribe. It is only to that extent that the Indian * Act is affected, not generally at all. Further than that, we only ask power to effect a settlement in accordance with the terms and principles set up, and modified by the negotiations. I-t will he our purpose that the modifications will be just as slight as possible. We are prepared to accept the report now; we do not want to modify it at all; -so from our point of view the modifications will be as slight as possible. 1 do not contend or think that the Act would give us power to expend money. We would have -to come to Parliament in the case of any readjustment involving the passing of money. I do not think there is any money to pass at all, except in this way, that -when a certain cut-off from a reserve is sold, in pursuance of -the recommendations of the report, half the proceeds from the sale will go to the province of British Columbia. That is -one of the terms of the report which is now before Parliament, an-d which we must abide -by if we accept that feature of the report, as we are prepared to do. The money must come, of course, before it is -paid out. -
-Mr. McIvENZIE:	I understand that the
land is now held by the Dominion Government in trust for the Indians, and that a reversionary interest is claimed by -the province of British Columbia. I have not been able to follow the machinery, but, of course, -somebody must be put in a position to give title to this land when it is sold. Does the province of British Columbia

agree to surrender their title to somebody who with the assistance of this Government will be in a position to give title to the purchaser? Has the minister arranged for the machinery by which title can be given to this land jwhen it is sold?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There can be no difficulty about the title for the reason that section 13 of the Act -of Union, of July 20, 1871, provides that the province of British Columbia shall transfer to the Dominion out of its own domain reserves for the Indians. They have done so. Consequently, we assert, and with undoubted right in my judgment, that title is in the Dominion. They contend that we enjoy that title only as trustees for the Indians, and that if we sell, if the Indians move away, the proceeds are theirs. We hope to effect a settlement with them on that point. They can make no claim to title. We say the Indian can make no claim to title, that the title is ours. We will simply grant patent on the sale of any portion or *all of the reserve. Of course, the Indians themselves of British Columbia have for a very long time been setting up a claim to aboriginal title in that province, but we cannot dispose of that question in this Bill. The Dominion claims title freed entirely from aboriginal claims, and the Dominion will give patent to these lands when sold. Surely that would be just as good title as the Dominion has been giving for forty years for land in the railway 'belt and the Peace River District, for example.
About what is the acreage and value of the cut-offs?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The total cut-offs amount to 47,058.49 acres. We have had two valuations, and according to one estimate, the total value is $1,522,704.72, and according to the other $1,247,912.72. The net increases of acreage are 87,291.17-a great deal more acreage than the cut-offs, but the value is only about one-quarter as much, namely, $444,838.80.
Mr. J. H. (SINCLAIR: The minister says that the province of British Columbia is claiming a reversionary interest in the proceeds of these land sales. Assuming that they are entitled to reversionary interest, will other provinces have the same rights in relation to Indian lands that are sold?
iytr. MEIGHEN: No. The grounds upon which the province of British Columbia bases its claim for reversionary interest do not exist in relation to the other provinces.
They arise by reason of the terms of section 13 of their Act of Union, and orders
passed.
Does the province claim a reversionary interest in the reserves of the railway belt?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: From memory, I think it does, but of that I am not very certain.

My recollection is that there is a distinction between the reserves in the railway belt and those outside on account of the transfer by the province under the terms of Union. I think the question has been raised, but I have never heard that it has been decided.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It has never been decided, that is certain.
About what percentage of the Indians have consented to this transaction? Have any of them consented, or are they all opposed to parting with these lands?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Indians, as Indians, are wards of the Government. They have not been approached with a view to obtaining their assent to an adjustment of claims as between the Dominion and Provincial Governments. I do not think it makes much difference to them. We recognize our responsibility to take care of the Indians as wards wholly.
The wards have rights as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly, we take care of all the rights of the Indians as wards; we recognize that duty. As to the matter of a reversionary interest in the Indian reserves, that is a claim of the province of British Columbia. In fact, it does not make much difference what stand any one takes, for it is a matter of the law on the rights of the Government and of the Indians.

The Indians must be interested in any change taking away from them 47,000 acres of land in one place and giving them instead 87,000 acres somewhere else. But is it not customary for the Government to get the consent of Indians before they ask them to leave any reserve? In this case, have they been consulted?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They are not leaving
any reserves except in the case of Kitsilano. In that case they did surrender. Under the Indian Act we must always obtain surrenders before the Indians give up possession at all, or even the right to cut wood

upon reserves. But for the purpose of obtaining a settlement-in the finality, not affecting the Indian rights at all, because the Indians are undoubtedly getting every thing that is coming to them-it is absolutely essential that we be able to take proper action and consequently we ask for power to do so without the necessity of sur-' render. If the necessity of surrender were interposed there would be no way of carrying this out at all, and I am at a loss to comprehend how the question is ever to be settled otherwise. The Kitsilano Reserve is occupied to-day by the Harbour Commissioners and not a dollar is paid for it for the simple reason that there is no place to pay it to. The Indians consequently have not the benefit of the money that is due them because it is not in our hands to give them. It is imperative that we should come to some settlement of this matter if the Indian is not to suffer, and this is the method we are desirous to adopt.

Does this apply only to
the reserves in Vancouver mentioned by the minister? This 47,000 acres is not all in one reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

Are other reserves in a
similar condition to that of the Kitsilano Reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Kitsilano Reserve
has been surrendered because in that case the Indians have been moved up to another reserve, Saanich. In the other cases it is merely an adjustment of reserves. Lands which the Indians are not using are being taken over and they are given new lands.
Are they satisfied?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think their
consent has been asked for in this case. We doubtless will obtain it in every possible case, but if it is to be made a condition precedent, then there is no use in passing this legislation.

The transferring of Indians from one place to another might be an advantage to them in the opinion of the minister, while the Indians might regard it in altogether a different light. The question is, are they satisfied? It is not a question whether the Government is satisfied, but are the Indians themselves satisfied that the transfer should be made, in other cases than that in Vancouver?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Generally speaking, I think they are. I do not know of any

specific objections to the action that has been taken. At any rate, I have not heard of any.

I take it that the Kitsilano lands were subject to the same laws regarding title as every other Indian reserve. Some years ago we heard a great deal in this House about the Kitsilano incident, and were informed, possibly correctly, that the habitations of the Indians were burnt, everything which they had in the shape of dwellings having been destroyed, with the result that they were forced off the land. I cannot recall what was done in the matter, but apparently, from the words of the minister, possession has been taken by the harbour commissioners. I do not suppose that the harbour commissioners forcibly dial edged the Indians and wrested the title from the trustees; I do not imagine that such a thing would be permitted in a civilized country. I should be .glad to know, however, how the commissioners got possession of the land and how they secured title without having paid for it. No doubt the harbour commissioners are a corporate body, and they are in the enjoyment of lands formerly occupied by the Indians, of whom the last we heard was that they 'had been virtually driven off by force. Perhaps the minister will explain how it is that the Government of Canada surrendered the title and gave patents to this corporation without any money having been paid. What arrangement has been .made in the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I can give from memory a fairly accurate account of the Kitsilano matter, from which the hon. member will see just how the harbour commissioners came to be in possession. First of all, let me say that I do not recollect any contention having been raised in this House that the Indians were not well treated. On the contrary, I do remember the contention being very strongly pressed that they were a little too well treated. They had too much money in their own hands, and treated themselves pretty well in consequence. The harbour commission felt that immediate possession was necessary, and the Government of British Columbia, in the interests of the city of Vancouver and the province generally, as well as harbour improvement there, were most anxious that surrender should be obtained. They obtained it, no doubt feeling that they had a certain authority in view of their claim to reversionary interest. At all events, they went about obtaining surren-

der and claimed to have paid the Indians between $200,000 and $3W,000 as part of the surrender value, and the Indians did actually surrender the land. At the same time the Royal 'Commission that was in operation made an interim report regarding the Kitsiiano reserve, recommending that that reserve be temporarily occupied by the harbour commission, and that the Government of Canada and the Government of British Columbia proceed to arbitrate the value of (the reserve and the value of the province's reversionary interest therein. The Government of Canada concurred in that interim report, and agreed, by means of correspondence with the Government of British Columbia, that whatever might be the finding of the arbitration as to the value of the province's reversionary interest, British Columbia should in no event receive less than $300,000, that being estimated as the amount to be paid by the province for the surrender, together with interest and expenses connected therewith. The subject matter then went to arbitration and the board of arbitration, found that the land was worth-if I remember correctly- $662,000. The Indian Department took exception to the finding, so did the Government of British Columbia; they claimed it was too low. An appeal was entered and went before Chief Justice Hunter of the province of British Columbia, who upset the arbitration proceedings not on the ground that the valuation was too low, or that there had been a failure to take account of relevant evidence, but rather on the ground that the province of British Columbia was not represented before the arbitration board. That simply threw us all hack to nowhere. We have no finding. Since that time we have been attempting to settle the matter. We had, as I thought, arrived at terms of settlement once but they were not final in the minds of both parties to the settlement in a way that we could usefully follow out. Therefore, we have not arrived at a settlement yet, and we are still in process of negotiation. The Government of British Columbia insists upon a much higher valuation of the property. The Government of Canada was willing, and is willing yet, that the province of British Columbia shall receive that sum of $300,000 out of the proceeds. I am now in communication with the attorney general of the province and I am in hopes that we will be able to arrive at some settlement of this outstanding dispute as a result. The Harbour Board has evidenced its .willingness to pay- I think a figure of-$750,000, that being
suggested by way of settlement. No settlement has yet been arrived at but immediately it is we are prepared to carry it out and to provide title and the Harbour Board stands ready at any time to pay the amount.

Has the Harbour
Board still to pay something in addition to what it has already paid to the Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Harbour Board has not paid anything. The province of British Columbia has paid the Indians between $200,000 and $300,000.

I am not quite sure
that we should allow this Act to go through without having something to say. It is new law to me, as I am sure it is to the hon. the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen), that a person who claims a reversionary interest has the right to go in and take possession of the 'property. The reversionary interest goes to the person who really holds it after the person who had held it dies. The land was in possession of the Indians, it was occupied by the Indians and a trust was exercised by this Government. The only right that the Government of British Columbia had was a vague, statutory reversionary interest which had not received judicial interpretation. It strikes me as a very highhanded proceeding that the Government oi British Columbia should take possession of the property, deprive the Indians of the use of it and say:	"There is a sum of
money; take it and get out." It is a most extraordinary proceeding and one which this Government should not recognize at Nall. They should have dealt with this property from the beginning under the terms of the Act and they should have discouraged 'high-handed proceeding of that kind on the part of any one.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On the motion of Hon. Newton W. Rowell (Minister of Health) Bill No. 27 respecting Food and Drugs was read the second time and the House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 2-definitions:

I note that in subsection (c) the word "domestic" is used to qualify the word "animal." The subsection reads:
(c) "drug" includes all medicines for internal or external use for man or for any domestic animal.
Sometimes wild animals are kept in captivity and are possibly treated with drugs.

I do not see why the -word "domestic" is put there. It limits the application of the Act. It does not fulfil any useful purpose. In a part of the country which is ably represented in this House foxes are raised for commercial purposes. I presume some of them occasionally get sick. If they are . domestic animals I suppose they will fall under this law. If they are not regarded as domestic animals, and I do not think they are, they would not fall under this law. It seems to me that there is no necessity for the word "domestic."

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Act as it now stands is broadened by this Bill but I see no objection to striking out the word "domestic." The word "animal" will include all animals. I therefore beg to move that the word "domestic" be stricken out in the 16th line of clause 2.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

Paragraph (d) in the definition of food sets forth that it:
includes every article used for food or drink-
I want to call the minister's attention to that-
-by man, and every ingredient intended for mixing with the food or drink of man for any purpose whatever;
Now is whiskey a food, and are we committing ourselves to that definition? Because it is a scientific question as ,to whether whiskey is food or not, and we do not want to commit ourselves to any dangerous admission.
Whiskey is a poison.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I wish to ask the minister if I am right in understanding that this Bill is brought down as a consolidation of the Acts already on the Statutes.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The existing Adulteration of Foods Act covers many matters in addition to the adulteration of food. It was passed many years ago and after several amendments the legislation was consolidated in 1906. Since then, it has been amended in many respects, and several new Acts have been passed dealing with different subject matters which are covered by the present Adulteration Act, and by reason of there being several Acts relating to the same subject matter there is confusion and difficulty in administration. In the present Bill we have eliminated all those matters that are provided for by other Acts and perhaps I might enumerate them so that the Committee will have these mat-

ters before them as we go through the Bill. The former Act in addition to dealing with foods and drugs proper, dealt with agricultural fertilizers. That class of products has since been .dealt with by a separate Act and therefore it passes out from the present measure. Proprietary and patent medicines were covered by an Act passed last session, therefore no provision is made in the present Bill for proprietary and patent medicines. Honey was also dealt with by the former Act, but hon. gentlemen will recall that a special Bill was put through the House the other evening in reference to that product. The former Act also dealt with maple products, but a separate Bill is before the House to-day covering that commodity. The old Act also dealt with commercial feeding stuffs and animal foods such as bran, shorts and middlings. Those are all likewise dealt with in a separate Bill now before the House. The present measure is therefore confined to foods and drugs. In that respect it simplifies the situation and will make the administration of the law much easier than it is at present. In addition, the existing law does not draw any clear . distinction between the adulteration and misbranding. Members of the Committee will see there is a clear distinction between putting some ingredient in a food -a deleterious substance which may be injurious to health,

and describing an article by some name other than it really is no doubt for the purpose of getting profit. But where the article is itself good for food and the only objection is that it is not accurately described, this Bill draws a clear distinction between the two things-adulterating, putting something in or taking something out which may be injurious, and misbranding; that is describing an article on the package or on the article itself in a way to deceive or mislead the public. The other changes I can perhaps more clearly indicate as we proceed with the Bill. The Act has been under administration for some twenty or thirty years and the proposed legislation embodies improvements which have been found necessary in actual operation by the department presided over by Dr. McGill. As we come to the different clauses I shall indicate as clearly as I can where the changes are made.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It will expedite discussion very much if the minister will deal with every new point in that way while the Bill is being considered because going through these different Acts is a very

laborious business. I would like to ask the minister one other question: a number of representations have been made by druggists from different parts of the country with respect to what they regard as somewhat drastic legislation in the matter of drugs. speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The representations relate to the Opium and Drug Act and I have intimated that that measure will not be proceeded with until after the iGovernment has heard the representations which those who will be affected by the legislation wish to make in regard to it.
On paragraph (e)-" inspector "

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I move to amend para-grah (e) by striking out the words " appointed by His Majesty " and substituting therefor the words " duly appointed by or on behalf of the Dominion Government
This is a suggestion made by the Department of Justice for the improvement of the paragraph as it now stands. In its present form the paragraph reads:
"inspector" means any person, appointed by His Majesty or by a municipality for the purpose of carrying- out the provisions of this Act.
Does the language used in the paragraph not always imply His Majesty?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I should have thought myself the amendment was not necessary, but in going over the Bill the Department of Justice suggested to me that it might be made.

"By the Dominion Government" is a very unusual expression in an Act. However, we all know what it means and that is perhaps the important feature of any legislation. The whole theory of the Government is that all appointments emanate from His Majesty.
We are now a nation.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As I have already said
I approved of the clause in its present-form thinking it was suitable for the purpose designed, but the Department of Justice, in finally passing upon it, suggested the modification in question. I think perhaps "the Government of Canada" is preferable to "the Dominion Government." I would therefore suggest that we change the wording to read "appointed by or on behalf of the Government of Canada,''
Is the minister giving power to a municipality to make an appointment of this kind?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: -We do not give municipalities such power; they appoint their own inspectors. A municipality has the power to appoint inspectors to deal with laws relating to that municipality.

May I point out before we get away from this 'paragraph that as the minister proposes to amend it the inspection must be made by an inspector appointed either by the Dominion Government or by a municipality? But if there are inspectors appointed by the province the term "inspector" would not cover such provincial inspection. Perhaps that is the intention; I merely draw attention to that point as it has occurred to me.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Just before I answer my hon. friend, I inadvertently misinformed my hon. friend from Cape Breton. Section 11 of the Act deals with inspectors appointed by councils. It provides:
The Council of any city, town, county or village or other municipality may appoint one or more inspectors of food or drugs, etc.
These appointments are therefore expressly provided for.

Would the minister explain who is to make these appointments? The paragraph says:
"Inspector" means any person appointed by or on behalf of, etc.
Who will make the appointment on behalf of the iGovernment if the Government do not make the appointment themselves?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
All these appointments
are made by the -Civil Service Commission under the existing law.

I should think that
the words " by His Majesty or by a municipality " might be left out and the clause .made to read:
" Inspector " means any person duly appointed for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of this Act.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have no objection to
the change; it seems to cover exactly the same ground. I move an amendment to that effect.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
i On section 4-drug, when deemed to be adulterated:

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
1 Mr. ROWELL:	The present Act refers
to a specific edition of the pharmacopoeia; which is now out of date. In this Bill the reference is to the latest edition of the British or of any foreign pharmacopoeia. Then subsection 2 provides that if it is not specified that the drug is to be judged by some other standard, the British Pharmacopoeia shall be the standard by which the drug shall be tested and with which it must comply-

What have we to do
with any foreign pharmacopoeia?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We have very substantial importations' of drugs from France, and we recognize the French Pharmacopoeia.
I Mr. FOURNIER: The codex.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, it is the standard
which the French have fixed for testing the purity of their drugs, and that standard is recognized here.
, Section agreed to.
On section 5-food, when deemed to be misbranded:	,
-	Mr. NESBITT: Paragraph (f) of section 5 says:
If in package form, sealed by the manufacturer or producer, and bearing his name and address, the contents of each package are not conspicuously and correctly stated in terms of weight, measure or number, upon the outside of the package.
-	I have a letter which draws my attention to the fact that many packages of perfectly pure foods which will not be sold within the year do not comply with this provision, and would be deemed to be misbranded. What has the minister to say about that?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I intend before the Bill
leaves the committee to move an amendment in this connection. I have not yet decided the exact form in which to submit it, but it will provide either that the Act shall come into force on proclamation, or, as was done in the case of the Patent Medicine Act of last session, that the Governor in Council may make regulations governing the disposal of existing stocks. There is no intention to confiscate property which was legitimately acquired under the existing law.
, Paragraph (a) of this section is substantially the same as the provision of the present law; it formed part of the adulteration clause. These words have been added: " and if it is not clearly and explicitly described as an imitation." Hon. members

will see the reason for that provision; if it is explicitly described as an imitation, then it is not misbranded. Paragraph (b) is a new clause. Paragraph (c) is also new: " If it is sold or offered for sale by a name which belongs to another article."
i Mr. FIELDING:	Is that a workable
clause? In the case of an article protected by trade mark there would be no difficulty. But suppose two articles of the same nature, bearing the same name but coming from different sources, are offered for sale, which one is the offender, neither being protected by trade mark? Two different concerns might easily produce substantially the same article. No doubt these things have all been carefully considered by the officials of the department. I desire to do no more than call attention to them.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think that the subsection is not intended to cover the specific point my hon. friend has in mind, though 1 can quite see the difficulty which might follow if it did deal with a case of that kind. It is intended to deal with the selling of an article under a name different from the real name of the article-in other words, an article which is misbranded.
Mr. FIELDING):	The question is, to
which of the two in the case I mentioned does tips provision apply?

This provision goes even further than my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) suggests. It says:	" If it is sold
or offered for sale by a name which belongs to another article." The name might belong to another article not at all similar to the article sold.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I should draw the attention of my hon. friends to the provisions of clause 14 which has a direct bearing on this. Clause 14 provides that:
The Governor in Council shall have power to make regulations,-
(a) prescribing standards of quality for and fixing the limits of variabilities permissible in any article of food or drug the standard of which is not otherwise prescribed by this Act;
(5) requiring a label to be attached, in such manner as he may direct, tq any article of food or drug, and prescribing what the colour, size and contents of such label shall be; '
(c) prescribing, in the case of foods in packages, sold at retail in such packages, what the shape and size of such package shall be, and of what material it shall be made.
I think perhaps sub-clause (a) might be made clearer. I understand from the officers of the department that in their view sub-clause (a) covers the matter:

Prescribing standards for and fixing the limits of variabilities permissible in any article of food.
The word "food" would cover the matter. This clause had better stand.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If sub-clause (c) Of clause 5 were made to read:
If it is sold or offered for sale by the name that belongs to It.
That would cover it.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That would appear to
cover it.

Before we pass from this clause, might I point out to the minister the possibility of confusion, and, I am afraid, trouble with regard to subclause (b) which reads:
If It is stated to be the product of a place or a country of which it is not truly a product.
There are in commerce a good many names which have acquired a secondary meaning. For instance, there is Belfast Ginger Ale. I am afraid that some zealous inspector, duly appointed, might possibly think that under sub-clause (b) he would have the right to proceed against some manufacturer who was manufacturing Belfast Ginger Ale. There is a danger in that clause, and I should like to hear what the minister has to say about it.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This clause is intended to meet cases where a certain foreign product has a well known character and reputation in the market and is bought by reason of that. It is not in the public interest, nor in the interest' of people who buy, that other products which are not made in that country and have not the quality, should be sold under that name. For instance, I might mention Java coffee and other commodities.

Would India curry
powder have to be made in India?
Mr. ROWEfLL: I am not familiar with that particular commodity. If a well known brand of powder of that character is made in India and known in our market, then the product of a similar kind made in Canada should not be sold under the name "India," because that would lead people to believe they were getting the product produced in India.
Would Washington coffee have to be made in Washington and Paris Green in Paris?
And what about Hamburg steak?
Would it be possible under sub-clause (a) to sell oleomargarine as a substitute for butter?
Sub-clause (a) does not prohibit the sale of oleomargarine if it be described as what it really is.
If it were described as imitation butter, would it be possible to sell it?

I think some alteration should be made in sub-clause (e) of clause 5, which reads:
If false or exaggerated claims are made for it upon the label or otherwise.
In trade what is an exaggerated claim? Supposing for instance, a man is selling soda biscuits, and on the label he has printed: "The biscuits contained in this package are superior in quality to those manufactured by any other firm in Canada." Literally that might be untrue, but the courts of this country regularly recognize what is known as puffing, and they distinguish between puffing and a false statement. For instance, a man has a perfect right under the law to say: "The biscuits contained in this package are the best manufactured in Canada." A man has also a perfect right to say: "That is the best piano manufactured in Canada," although it may be a very inferior piano. That is regarded by the courts as simply puffing, and every man who sells anything has a right under the law to make a general statement of that kind as distinguished from a mis-statement of a fact. If a man says: "The biscuits contained in this package are made from number one hard Manitoba wheat and that was not the case, that is a definite, false statement and is contrary to general law. But in a general sense a man has a perfect right to say that such and such is the best material of the kind manufactured, although that may not be actually true. Under this sub-clause, if it is left as it stands, who is going to determine whether the vendor has exaggerated the qualities of a particular article or not? 1 think this should be either stricken out altogether or modified to a matter of actual fact capable of being proved, and not a matter of opinion.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The party to determine
the matter would be the magistrate before whom the ease came for adjudication, but I appreciate the difficulty of using such a word as "exaggerated." The department has encountered difficulties in enforcing the

law, and the officers of the department were very anxious to have something to enable them to reach parties who were real offenders. On the other hand, one can conceive the difficulty that my hon. friend has pointed out, of puffing, which is perhaps not a desirable thing but which is very common, being construed as coming within the provisions of the law. It may be that we go far enough at present if we simply provide:
If false claims are made for it upon the label or otherwise.
I am quite willing to strike out the words "or exaggerated," and try out the provision in the meantime simply on the basis of false claims.
Is the minister going to strike out subclause (c)?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I should like to let subclause (c) stand in order to discuss with the officers of the department just what effect the change might have. At present I consider the suggestion of the leader of the Opposition would cover the matter.
If the words "of fact" were inserted after the word "claims" in clause (e), there would be no question about the matter being one of opinion.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Sub-clause (a) seems to be contradictory. It does not seem to be advisable to permit any article being sold as something other than what it really is, and sub-clause (a) allows you to do that. Why should we allow a man to sell an article that is an imitation? In the first place, the word " imitation" implies that some man is trying to sell something under a guise or a camouflage, if he sells it as an imitation. Why should we countenance that at all? For instance, a man might put on a package of oleomargarine the words " pure creamery butter," and then in very small letters underneath "but really oleomargarine." That would be a perfectly legitimate thing to do. When a man buys a railway ticket a great number of conditions are printed on the back, but how many men read those conditions, or the conditions of a fire insurance policy? Under this clause it would seem to me that oleomargarine could be sold as pure butter simply by putting the word "oleomargarine" in small type underneath. Why should we allow anybody to sell an imitation, even in the case of a necessary article of food? .
Section stands.
On section 6-compounds, mixtures, etc., to be labelled as such, and not to be marked "pure," "genuine," etc.:

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Let me illustrate the kind of case this clause is designed to meet. An article, take mustard, for instance, may be put on the market and may be quite wholesome but not pure mustard. The mustard may have a certain amount of flour mixed with it. Similarly with many other commodities that are sold on the market. We are providing that if the word " pure " or " genuine " is used, it must be the genuine article. If they wish to sell an article that is not wholly composed of the substances described on the label, they must not use the words " pure " or " genuine."- This is simply to prevent the public from being misled by the use of these words.

What objection would there be to having the manufacturers indicate on . the label the composition' of the article? A druggist never objects to writing the prescription on the label of a bottle of medicine, if requested, but when it comes to food we allow any one to sell any kind of food under a false name. I should like to know if there is any real objection to having my suggestion carried out? .

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My_ hon. friend will see that there would be serious objection to it in the case, for instance, of commodities which are good articles of food but the composition of which is a frade secret. If there is nothing misleading about the name, there seems to be no necessity for stating the ingredients on the label. My hon. friend is mistaken in thinking that the druggists are required to write the prescription on the label.
He had in mind proprietary medicines.

Where there is no trade
secret to be given away, I do not see why the public should not be told what the ingredients are.

My hon. friend (Mr. Middlebro) will find his criticism respecting the use in large type of the words "pure creamery butter " and in smaller type the word " oleomargarine " covered, I think, by this clause, which provides that:
Every article of food which is a compound, mixture, imitation or substitute shall be plainly and correctly labelled as such; and the words " pure " or " genuine " or words equivalent to these terms, shall not be used on the labels or in connection with such articles, and such articles shall be so packed, marked or labelled as not to be likely to deceive any person with respect to their true nature.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.

On section 7-samples may be obtained:

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Subsection (1) is substantially the existing law. Subsections (2) and (3) are important, and I think should be brought to the attention of the committee. Subsection (2) is rendered necessary by reason of the fact that in cases where an inspector has no reasonable doubt about a certain article being adulterated food, in order to justify his taking action he must take a sample and have it analyzed, and under the law as it now stands it is very doubtful if he has a right to require that the bulk shall be detained until that analysis has been made. As a matter of practice, the department is detaining the bulk until.the analysis can be made, but we are advised by our officers that it is desirable that that right should be made perfectly clear, so that in the meantime the adulterated food cannot get out of reach of the department.
Subsection (3) is intended to protect us against the importation of adulterated food. I am advised that in the past there have been many cases where adulterated foods which should not be exposed for -ale in this country have, been imported from cut-side. Hon. members will see that the right to examine is limited. The inspector must have the direct authority of the minister before he can examine customs entries and detain food until an analysis can be made. The officials of the department say that both these provisions are very important for the efficient administration of the law and for the protection of the public.

As the minister has
explained, provision is made that an embargo may be laid on imports until an analysis can be made. Then the clause goes on to provide that if " the food or drug is adulterated or misbranded, such food or drug shall not be admitted into Canada for use as a food or drug." For what other purposes than as a food or drug would it be admitted?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There are a number of
uses to which an article may properly be put, and some cases have come up within the past few months in the administration of the department. Albumen of egg, which is not suitable for human food, may be used for tanning purposes, and there are certain manufacturing processes in which commodities such as this may be used. I know that within the past five or six months a large quantity of some article imported into Canada for food was seized by the department. It would cleo''1" have been in-61
jurious to health to have that article marketed a;S food, but it was quite useful in some manufacturing business and we therefore permitted its employment for that purpose.
That seems reasonable, but has the minister the machinery by which he can guarantee that an article, having been once imported as food, may be used only for a manufacturing purpose?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In the case I have in
mind we took bonds from responsible parties before releasing the article. Whether or not we had the authority to do it we detained the article, a large quantity of which had been imported. The analyst having decided that it was unfit for food, we deemed it wise, instead of detroying the article, to take bonds frbm responsible parties guaranteeing that it would not be used for any other than specified purposes.

I quite agfee that an
article which may be unfit for food may serve a very useful manufacturing purpose, but I think the minister should have some machinery that will insure the safety of the public. Unless there is adequate machinery you may find that an article which is condemned as food, but which is permitted to be used for mechanical purposes, may eventually find its way back to the1 shop and be exposed for sale as human food.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think we have the
power under the section regarding regulations. If not, I shall bear in mind the hon. member's suggestion.

It is a common practice when goods which are imported for food are found to be unfit for that purpose to deem them as being illegally in the country and to confiscate them. There does not seem to be any ppwer of confiscation here. Suppose a man who imported goods that were found to be unfit should refuse to give such a bond as the minister has spoken of, what would be done in the matter?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is a power of forfeiture under section twelve.

But what about the
power to authorize the use of goods for other than food purposes?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Under sections fourteen and fifteen there is a general authority to make regulations, and subsection "D" of section fifteen provides "for carrying out the provisions of this Act." When we come to that subsection, which is very .broad, I shall consider the point raised by my hon.



friend, if there is found to be any necessity for modification.
Subsection "D" of section fifteen does not help the minister in making regulations. There must be a previous provision in regard to the disposal of condemned goods.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Section 12 provides for
this.
12. (1) Whenever any article of food or any drug is reported hy a Dominion analyst as being adulterated or misbranded within the meaning of this Act, the department may order such article and all other articles of the same description which were in the same place at the time the article analysed was obtained to be seized by an inspector and detained by him until an analysis of a sample of the whole is made.
(2) If the Dominion analyst reports to the department that the whole or any part of such articles of food or drugs as have been submitted for analysis by the aforesaid inspector is adulterated or misbranded, the Minister may declare such articles, or so much thereof as the Dominion analyst reports to be adulterated or misbranded, to be forfeited to the Crown, and they shall be forfeited accordingly, and may be disposed of as the minister directs.

They are disposed of
after forfeiture.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, as the minister may direct. I shall keep my hon. friend's point in mind.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section eight-Inspector has to deal with samples.

This section provides
for court proceedings and enacts that the certificate of the analyst shall be received as evidence in any proceedings taken against any person in pursuance of this Acf. This might be a good way for an officer to get in evidence, but I need hardly remind my hon. friend that evidence of this nature is exceedingly unpopular. The best way to prove a case is the ordinary old-fashioned way of- producing iwitnesses and having the whole matter aired before the court.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In that respect the law is not materially changed, except that the certificate may be the certificate of a " Dominion Analyst " instead of the " Chief Analyst." My hon. friend will see that this is a case where the government official has no object whatever other than to get at the actual contents of the article examined or analysed. If he makes an examination and finds the article adulterated his certificate is put in as evidence in the 
case. Having regard to the objects for which the legislation is being enacted, I think it is very desirable that provision should be made to make the enforcement of the law expeditious and convenient. Suppose that the defendant in a case was in a position to show that a mistake had been made, there would be no object in the department prosecuting. All they wish to do is to get at the facts. Section 9 also provides that:
(1)	If the person who supplied the article respecting which the certificate referred to in the last preceding section is given, deems himself aggrieved thereby, he may within ten days of the receipt of the copy of such certificate furnished to him, notify the minister in writing that he intends to present evidence in his own behalf to controvert the certificate of the Dominion analyst, stating in full the nature of such evidence. In the absence of such notice the certificate of the analyst shall be taken as final.
He is not precluded from giving evidence but he must give notice beforehand to enable the department to meet the case. Then sub-section 2 of section 9 provides:
(2)	Should the evidence submitted by the person above referred to be such as in the opinion of the Chief Dominion Analyst to justify further investigation, the Chief Dominion Analyst may cause the second part of the sample submitted to the Department, as provided in section eight, to be analysed to his satisfaction, and a certificate of such analysis signed by the Chief Dominion- Analyst shall be final and conclusive evidence of the facts therein set out.
The sample is taken away, it is divided ' into three parts and it is only the analysis of the actual sample taken that can be used as the basis of prosecution. Otherwise the man charged might substitute something else and say that that was the article he had at the time the seizure was made. I think ample protection is given by section 9 to meet the case mentioned. I should point out that sections 8^ and 9 are substantially the present law with two exceptions. Section 8, sub-section 4 provides, that:
A copy of such certificate shall be furnished by the department to the person from whom the sample was procured within six months of the time of procuring the sample.
There was no provision in the Act as it stood that the certificate should be furnished within any definite time and it is only reasonable that a man from whose goods a sample is taken for analysis should have the certificate furnished within some fixed time. Provision is also made that the certificate of the Dominion analyst may be taken in the first instance rather than the

certificate of the chief Dominion analyst. It would be quite impossible for the chief analyst to personally analyse all the samples taken.
Why should a man have to wait for six months to get that certificate.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He does not have to wait; it is furnished in due time, or as soon as it is available. This is simply a limitation upon the existing law.

Has there not been
found a difficulty in that samples are taken say, from a grocer's shop? He does not make the goods at all; he buys them in good faith and sells them in good faith. Is it the intention to proceed to examine samples of the product of the manufacturer, the source from which the goods come? It does seem a hardship that the grocer who buys an article in all good faith, believing he is getting the correct thing, upon it being discovered that there is some adulteration, must be pilloried before the public through no fault of his own. It may be that there is no other way of getting at it, but I have known cases in which there has been very great hardship.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I appreciate the point raised by the hon. gentleman and in order to get over the difficulty provision is made to reach the manufacturer and as far as possible to take samples from him. But it has been found in many cases that the only way to reach the trouble has been to go into a store, actually buy an article and take a sample. Provision is made in section 17 for the case which my hon. friend has mentioned where a man might plead want of knowledge and thereby escape the consequences of his act.

He escapes the consequences in the way of a penalty in the courts but in the meantime a bulletin has been issued by the department which practically blacklists the grocer who has sold that article. It is true the public do not generally see these bulletins; it is a pity they do not in some cases. I know of a ease where a gross injustice has been done to reputable merchants who have been pilloried in the bulletins of the department. I am not complaining of the department for doing this; I have no doubt they are only carrying out their duty, but it seems to me a very great hardship.

I absolutely agree with
what has been said by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). 614
Could not the Act be so framed that if an article were seized in a retail store, the manufacturer of the article would be responsible? You might force a manufacturer under this Bill to put his name on the article so that you would know exactly who made it and you could come back at him. I have known of instances where the retail man was just as innocent as a baby in the matter. He did not know that the article that he had sold was not what it was represented to be but still his name went forth to the public. This may hurt a man's business a great deal.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I may say in answer to both my hon. friends that while I believe in the past the course they have indicated was pursued, it is not now being pursued. No names are published in any bulletin until after a conviction is actually registered. The case that my hon. friends have mentioned would not arise in so far as publication in the bulletin is concerned.
Is the manufacturer not the man who is guilty and is he not the man who should be punished if there is any deception or wrongdoing?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will be glad to discuss the point when we come to section 17, which deals particularly with the matter.

If section 8 passes, section 17 will be ineffective. I sympathise very strongly with what has been said by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) and my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt). After all the man who produces the article, puts it in the can and sells it, is the man who knows what the contents of the receptacle are and he is altogether responsible to the public for what he puts up. Within the last few days an action for damages has been tried in one of the provinces. The complainant passed the retailer altogether and brought the action direct against the man who manufactured the goods. This is not a new principle at all as. it has been upheld both in England and in the United States. That being the case I should think it would be worthy of consideration by the minister as to whether or not he should always go after the manufacturer, and provide the means of reaching him.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The change proposed in line 7 of section 8 is merely a verbal one. The reference there given should be to section 16 instead of section 17.
'On section 10-analysis may be obtained of any sample:

iMr. MeKENZIE: What is really meant by " Dominion analyst '? Mr. MeKENZIE: Just a moment. I was drawing the minister's attention to the question of the qualification of an analyst. It is quite true that the Bill contains a definition of an analyst, but what I maintain is that we should be assured that these analysts have some standard qualifications, that they have taken a degree in some college or are recognized as holding some certificate, and that they are not simply appointees of the Government.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In answer to my hon. friend I would say that the qualifications for appointment to a position of this kind are determined under the classification of the Civil Service. A candidate for the position of analyst is required to have suitable educational qualifications; he must have graduated from a university or school and possess attainments qualifying him for the position. I have not got the prescribed qualifications under my hand at present, but I shall be glad to furnish my hon. friend with that information.
Mr. MeKENZIE: Must we go to the Civil Service Commission to get a definition of the qualifications of an analyst?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The qualifications are set forth in the classification submitted to the House at the last session of Parliament. When a position is vacant and the Civil Service Commission advertises, the particular qualifications required are specified in detail.
Mr. MeKENZIE: Under the provisions of the odd Civil Service Act a man could be appointed to a technical position in the Government service without the consent of the Civil Service Commission, but it may be otherwise now. If it is possible for a man without the necessary technical know-

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

Surely it should not be necessary, having regard to all the facilities at the disposal of the department, for a private person to take proceedings against a vendor for violation of the provisions of this Act. speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 11-inspectors appointed by councils:
Sections 10 and 11 provide that the offender can be prosecuted as well as the manufacturer, and that raises the question that was brought up by my hon friend (Mr. Fielding).

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As a matter of practical administration I am afraid that we cannot consent to limit the prosecution solely to the manufacturer. The department in every case endeavours to reach the parties primarily responsible. But it is a matter of great importance that adulterated food or drugs which are dangerous to the public health should not be sold; therefore it has been considered necessary that the department should have the right to proceed directly against the parties who sell, leaving it to them to establish their innocence.

The minister has stated that the Civil Service Commission would appoint inspectors provided for by paragraph (e) of section 2; but under section 11 the council of any city, town, county or village or other municipality may appoint inspectors. Is there not a conflict of authority here?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Dominion inspectors will be appointed by the Civil Service Commission. There is also the right on the part of local municipalities to appoint local inspectors. In fact, it is necessary that the principal municipalities at least should do so, otherwise we should have to have a corps of Dominion inspectors wtih a consequent unfair charge against the Federal exchequer. The local municipalities must take an interest in the enforcement of this law; therefore every encouragement is given to them to appoint their own inspectors, to initiate their own prosecutions and to get the benefit of the fines. The inspector has no right to give the certificate. He goes about, inspects and makes seizures, but his functions are quite different from that of the analyst.
Will the local inspectors have the same duties as the Dominion inspectors?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The local inspectors can only exercise the authority that is expressly given them. They may take the sample, but they must submit it to the Dominion analyst, and on the basis of the decision of the Dominion analyst as to the quality of the product a prosecution may be instituted.

I think it inadvisable to have in a Federal Act a statement which makes it appear that this Parliament is giving to a municipality the right to do such and such a thing. Consequently, it seems to me that the phrase, "The council of any city, town, county or village or other municipality may appoint," and so on, is unfortunate. I do not challenge the object which the clause seeks to attain, but it seems to me that it might better be worded: "Inspectors appointed by the council of any city, town, county or village," ;.nd so on. I would not in a Federal Act grant the right to municipal councils to do such and such a thing. This Parliament has no right to direct municipal councils to do or not to do such and such things, because municipal councils derive their power, not from the Dominion, but from the provinces.
Mr. BO WE'LL: I appreciate the point raised by my hon. friend. But this section has been in the law for over thirty years; we are only re-enacting what has been in the statute for a very long time. Frankly, when the Bill first came up, I was under the impression that all we were doing was recognizing the authority of inspectors appointed by the municipalities, but the Act itself goes further. I do not think any difficulty can arise from this. We are giving these inspectors, after they are appointed by the municipalities, certain powers. It is our function to give them those powers,

Once they are appointed, I agree with the minister that it is quite right for us to give them the powers, but the legislation goes further than that; it says in so many words: " The council of any city, town or village may appoint." I say that we have no right to say to a municipal council: " You may appoint an inspector." The only power that has the right to say that is the power vested in the province. I am inclined to think the minister will agree with me on that constitutional point.

I think under certain conditions we have power over municipalities just as we have power over individuals; but I do not think it is necessary to enter into a discussion of that constitutional question at present. The fact is that this has been in the law for thirty years, and the Department of Justice has approved this legislation in its present form. Therefore, I should say we are quite safe in leaving it as it is in that respect.
Under this measure will a municipal council have power to dismiss an officer?

These officers are wholly under the control of the municipalities. I have no hesitation in saying that had I drafted the law originally I should have provided that where the municipalities appointed these officials, these officials should have certain powers. But I do not think any harm can come from leaving this as it is.

This is not exactly the form in the original Act, but the difference is not in the point which my hon. friend has mentioned. The Act as it originally stood reads:
Such analyst shall, upon tender of the fees fixed for the analysis of such class of articles by the Governor In Council, forthwith analyse the same and give the inspector a certificate of the said analysis.
I should think a little more than tendering is required; payment is what is required.
Payment by the party applying. There is here almost the implication that the analyst has to make the payment. The fact, however, that this has been the law for thirty years, is good authority.

I should have thought
that the fact that this was on payment by the party applying was clearly implied from the clause, quite apart from its antiquity, and that it did not require its age to justify it. The clause reads:
Such Dominion Analyst shall, on payment of the prescribed fee.
That must be on payment of the fee for the analysis referred to in the preceding sub-clause, sub-clause (1) which says that the inspector may require a Dominion Analyst to analyse any samples of food or drugs procured by him. I have no objec-

tion to inserting the words " to him," if my hon. friend thinks that is necessary, hut I do not think it is necessary.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.

speechtext:

' Mr. McMASTER: I do not think that i* any improvement. I think the word ".description" keeps the matter closer to what is being seized. For instance, one sort of meat might be of the same character as another.

I absolutely* disagree with my hon. friend (Mr. McMaster) when he says that the word "description" is better than the word "character."

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I find that in the old
Act-and I confess I am not aware wby in drafting this Bill a change was made-the words are "the same kind and quality."

The words "the same
kind" would suit me.

speechtext: We had better adopt the description in the original Act. speechtext:
