Section as amended agreed to.
On section 14-regulations by Governor in Council.

I should like to draw the minister's attention to sub-clause (c). Those of us who are in business in this country have troubles enough without having any more thrown in our way. Why are such obstacles placed in the way of doing business? What is the sense of having the department say what size and what shape of packages food shall be put in? What difference does the shape or the size make or what material packages may be made of so long as they are not made of poisonous material? That is an unnecessary interference with trade, in my judgment, and might cause a great deal of expense to a manufacturer. He is the best judge of the most suitable size, because he has to cater to the trade. No man in the House of Commons, or in the department, would be as good a judge as to the size and shape of the package as the manufacturer, because it is his business to get the trade.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It has been found in the actual administration of the law that where an article of food put up in a certain sized package or container has acquired a high reputation on the market because of its character and quality, other manufacturers will put up a similar article, but of inferior quality, which they can afford to sell at a lower price, in substantially the same sized container or package, and the public in looking at the two is misled. The view of the department is that in such a case the inferior article should be sold in a different kind of package so that the public will not confuse it with the better known article of superior quality.
This clause does not touch that at all. The whole Act provides against imitation, but this clause regulates the size of package that all commodities shall be put up in.

I do not think any
special legislation is necessary to cover cases of the kind mentioned, because a man could

bring an action for unfair competition or passing off an article as something else.

I am not speaking oi
imitation. I say this clause gives power to prescribe the kind of package that every manufacturer shall put his stuff up in.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is not a power which the minister is compelled to use. It is only power to deal by regulation with a situation where it is believed that such regulation is necessary. It is not contemplated that there should be general regulations governing all kinds of packages, but it is desired by the department that there should be power to deal with the class of cases such as I have indicated, which have already arisen in the administration of the law.

Does the minister mean that if a manufacturer puts up a certain article in a certain kind of package the department will have power to say that another manufacturer shall not put up a similar article in a similar package?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No. A manufacturer
puts uip a certain article of a well-recognized standard or quality in a certain sized container, which becomes known to the public. When the article has become well-known on the market another manufacturer, knowing the reputation it has acquired, may produce a similar article of inferior quality which he can afford to sell at a lower price, and put it up in a container similar in general design and character to the other one, and the public are thereby misled. I am told that is the actual situation which sometimes arises in the administration of the law, and the sole object of the department is to take power to prevent the public from being misled into buying an article of inferior quality, thinking they are getting an article of better quality.

But the whole Act provides against imitation. This is an interference with trade. Biscuit manufacturers, for instance, from one end of the country to the other put- up a three-pound" package oi biscuits. It is exactly the same sized package all over the country, but they do not pretend for a minute to imitate some other manufacturer. It seems to me utterly incomprehensible to suppose that people would be deceived by articles being put up in a similar package. These packages have to have their own labels on, and by this Act the manufacturer is required to say whether the article is pure or adulterated. I repeat, this clause is an absolute interference with trade.

I do not think this
clause deals with quality, as suggested by the minister. His reasoning in the main is good, -but I think it would be stronger if he dealt mainly with the question of quantity. A lady, for instance, buys a certain article by the package; the package becomes a standard article. When you buy a package of this or that you do not make an analytical examination as to the weight. The package has a standard value, and as the minister states, an old established concern may have a reputation for its goods sold in that way, and some other manufacturer may put up another article-not of inferior quality, because I do not think that is touched on by this clause-in a similar package which he can afford to sell at a lower price, and that comes in competition with the old established article. I think in such a case this clause would have a very good effect. Where an article is well known and is sold by the package, without much analysis as to the weight, I think it is right and fair that nobody else should attempt to sell the same article in a similar sized package, and the Government should have the power to regulate the size of the package in which the article shall be sold. We regulate the weight of a barrel of flour. That is just as much an interference with trade, but we do it because the barrel is standardized and no one is allowed to sell, as a barrel, a less quantity than is prescribed. I think on the question of quantity rather than on quality the minister's argument is sound.

Might I point out to my hon. friend that we have already by this Act provided that the weight shall be put on the package so that the public shall not be deceived. Of course we regulate the weight of a bag of potatoes or a barrel of flour and many other things which are sold by the barrel or bag, but that is a different thing entirely. This clause deals with articles sold by the package.

I quite agree with my
hon. friend (Mr. Nesibtt). I think that paragraph (c) should be dropped entirely from the Bill. It is absolutely unnecessary. I speak from experience in matters of this kind. If a manufacturer has established a reputation for a certain article and another manufacturer comes along with an imitation in similar package, the first manufacturer has recourse against the other at law and can restrain him from interfering with his rights. This clause means that a manufacturer who produces a new article

must come to Ottawa for instructions from the department as to the size of the package in which that article shall be put up, the colour of the label, and all such minor details which he would arrange in his own office to suit his own convenience and to secure the success of his product on the market. I think the committee would be well advised to eliminate this section entirely.

I would ask the minister to regard this clause exactly as it should be regarded. This is not paternal legislation; it is not even maternal legislation; it is, I think, grandmotherly legislation. It is absurd that a department of government should have the right to say to a manufacturer:	" You shall not put
up your product in a tin that will hold two pounds, but in one that will hold five pounds; you shall not put it up in a tin coloured red, but in one coloured blue or grey, or some neutral colour; and you shall make your label of such and such material." I would ask the minister seriously to realize that all this interferes with the principles of liberty which people should enjoy in carrying on their business in the way they should judge best so long as they do not interfere with the acquired rights of others. It is a well-known principle of law, with which the minister is no doubt much more familiar than I am, that restraint will be put upon the man who dishonestly endeavours to avail himself of the goodwill or reputation that attaches to the goods of a competitor, and we had better leave the well laid down principles of law to regulate this matter. I see no great objection to subsection " A " of the clause, but I would ask the minister to strike out subsections " B " and " C," for I cannot see that they serve any useful purpose. The explanation given by the minister just shows how unfortunate the exercise of the power in question may be. Let us suppose that there are two manufacturers making a breakfast food, and that the superior breakfast food is oatmeal, which has been put up in a certain package for many years. Some man comes forward with cream of wheat or some other fancy breakfast food and, according to the minister, if he puts it up in a package similar to that which has contained rolled oats he may be told by the department that he has no right to put up his product in this way because it is an inferior breakfast food. The public having been accustomed to buy rolled oats in a certain package, he must not attempt *
to put up his cream of wheat in the same way. Well, it seems to me that that is reducing legislation to an absurdity. People who realize that oatmeal is an excellent food will buy oatmeal and those who want cream of wheat should be allowed to buy this article, no matter in what package the manufacturer cares to put it up. If there is unfair competition, and an attempt is made by a manufacturer or merchant to pass off his goods as those of another, then the law will restrain him, and this is the principle which I think should apply in this matter. There is a tendency in legislation to try to meet with a special law every specific case that arises. I think this is a mistake. It cumbers our statutes, and justice between man and man is not attained by placing these meticulous enactments upon the statute book.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The illustration which
my hon. friend Ipas given emphasizes the importance of certain foodstuffs in which he is very much interested,
Merely as a consumer.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
-his interest being no
doubt responsible for the vigour with which he discusses these questions; but it is entirely different from the illustration I gave to the House. I could not give a better illustration than that offered by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), and it is just to prevent frauds in such cases as he has mentioned, and others of a similar character, that the legislation is designed. I am quite prepared to let the clause stand if it can be modified in any way that will protect the public against being misled. There is no desire to hamper business, the sole object being to protect the public. I move that the section stand.
Section stands.
On section 15-regulations by minister:

The minister is taking large powers to himself. I agree that it is necessary that regulations should be made to carry out the purposes of the Act, but these regulations should be proposed by the minister and have the approval of the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Probably it is wiser to
put it in that form, and I therefore move to substitute for the word " minister " the words " Governor in Council."

"The minister, with
the approval of the Governor in Council," would do.
It comes to the same thing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why not consolidate this with the. previous section?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not sure that some of the details in connection with this section need be published in the Gazette. I prefer to leave the two sections separate. I move that " Governor in Council " be substituted for the word " minister " in the first line of section 15.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

What interpretation
does the minister place upon these words : " or otherwise given assistance leading to conviction in the case in question "? If the minister proposes to give half the fine to a witness who testifies, I object to that, as an unfortunate provision. I can understand that the informer should get half the fine. That is an encouragement which is given to informers but which is offset by public disapproval of this brand of gentry. But persons who " otherwise have given assistance " may, under this clause, get half the fine. If that refers to the lawyer who might conduct the prosecution in such a case I would have no harsh words to say to the minister, but I should not like this provision to extend to witnesses, who should be indemnified and not rewarded.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend will see
that this is to be covered by regulations which will define the conditions. Of course, it is not intended to give to a witness any compensation that would be improper, but it is necessary, in the adequate administration of the law, that advantage should be taken of information furnished, and where you give a portion of the fine it is an inducement in many cases for people to give information that may lead to prosecution under the Act. The information might come from more than one source. There might be different provisions in regard to the information furnished or the assistance given. That would all be covered by suitable regulations. I do not think there is any danger in that clause.

With the explanation of the minister before us I do not see any necessity for the words "or otherwise given assistance." The minister takes power with the consent of the Governor in Council to make regulations prescribing that a portion of the fine may go to the informer or to the person who has given information. I have no objection to that, but I cannot

see how any one else but the witness and the lawyers would give assistance to obtain a conviction.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have no objection to
limiting it to "any person who has given information leading to conviction in the case in question," striking out the words "or otherwise given assistance." I therefore beg to move to strike out the words "or otherwise given assistance."

I have never come
across any criminal proceedings or law cases -like this. The minister can find abundant cases where half the fine goes to the informer, but I -never saw any legislation going farther than that. That in itself is going as far as it should. We do not want any more informers. I think that provision should be struck out altogether. The question has to be determined by the magistrate who tries the case. If the Act says that half the fines shall go to the informer, it must mean the man who lays the information. There is no difficulty about that, but there -may be three or four other people who come before the court -and say that they are the people who gave the information that led to the conviction. There are only two halves, and if the court says that half of the fine shall go to the informer there will be no half to go- to these other people. This sort of legislation is not very commendable, but when it says that half of the fine shall go to any person who gives information that leads to securing a conviction, it is going: to cause a great deal of trouble.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have already intimated that I shall be content to move that the words "or otherwise given assistance" shall be stricken out. They were put in for the reason that it was thought they would be of benefit, but I am not going to press the point. Let me give -an illustration which has just been given to me from the officer administering the Act. Information comes to the department that a person professing to manufacture a certain commodity is in receipt of large quantities of another material which may be used as an adulterant. That is information upon which an investigation may be proceeded with. It may be that all the informant knows is that the commodity has been shipped in. That does lend assistance to the department in securing a conviction. That is what was in the mind of the officials of the department in suggesting these words. It is not direct information; it is only

information with regard to a fact that puts the department in a position to make inquiry; they follow it up and subsequently discover the main offence for which the man is prosecuted.

Is that not ususally
provided for,by some sort of a (Secret service fund? It should not he provided for by the court. Whether the minister knows it or not, there is such a fund, and moneys of that kind aTe being paid out from time to time for the enforcement of Acts.
It would furnish a great fund of criticism for an Opposition.

We furnish .a great
fund of information to the Government, and it is information which they seem to require. If there is any division of the fine to be made, that division must be made by the magistrate. It cannot he made by anybody else. It cannot be divided afterwards by the officer of the department; he has no jurisdiction. The magistrate must say in his conviction where the fine should go and this legislation must be such that the court enforcing it must know what is intended and what disposition shall be made of the fine.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: These words "or otherwise given assistance" are to be stricken out.

Before the section is
passed, there is another point that I would like some information on. Section 15, says: "Provided that no portion of any fine shall be paid to any Dominion analyst or to any inspector." Does that include inspectors appointed by the council of a city or other municipality? Do they come under that rule as well as the inspectors of the department in Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes; they do not get the benefit of that division of the fine. Section 11 provides in case of municipal inspectors that the fine in every case goes to the municipality to be used as the municipality may direct. Subsection 4 says:
All penalties Imposed and recovered at the suit of any such inspector, shall be paid into the revenue of the city, county, town or village by the council of which such inspector was appointed, and may be used in such manner as the council of such city, county, town or village may direct.
They may themselves provide that a portion may go to their own employee, but in so far as this legislation is concerned we
provide that the fine imposed as the result of a prosecution by a municipal inspector shall be paid to the municipality to be disbursed by themselves as they see fit.

I have a letter from a condensing company and they have the impression that it will not be legal for them to sell skim milk even if they mark the packages as skim milk. I would like to have that question cleared up if it is possible at this juncture.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know of anything in the Act which would prevent selling skim milk as skim milk.

At six o'clock the House resumed and then took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed in Committee consideration of Bill No. 27 respecting Food and Drugs.
On section 16-sale of adulterated or misbranded article, penalty.
Will the minister explain the provisions to this clause?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The clause does not differ in any material respect, from the provisions in the existing law, as I now recall them, except that it makes a difference in the penalty for an adulteration injurious to health-adulteration in which some poisonous substance or some substance deleterious to health is introduced into the food product -and for other violations of the law. Hon. members will see that the penalty is increased. The penalty is a fine not exceeding $500 and costs, and not less than $50 and costs, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months, or both fine and imprisonment, if the adulteration is injurious to health. If the adulteration is not injurious to health but still an adulteration

within the meaning of the Act, or if the article is misbranded, then the penalty for the first offence is a fine not exceeding $100 and costs and not less than $25 and costs, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months. Then, for each subsequent offence the penalty is made the same as in case of an adulteration injurious to health.

Who is going to benefit
by the fine?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If the fine is the result
of a prosecution instituted by the Government inspectors themselves, it goes to the revenue of Canada, unless in the cases expressly provided for, where it is as a result of information given that a conviction is secured. Then provision may .be made for one-half of the fine going to the party who gives the information. If the conviction is the result of a prosecution instituted by a municipal inspector-an inspector appointed by a municipality in connection with the administration of the Act-then the whole fine goes to the municipality to be disposed of as it may direct.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would like to point out to the minister that the clause as drafted seems to be very far-reaching indeed. Under it, if I am right, a merchant would be liable to a fine of $250 and costs, or imprisonment, simply for exposing in his window an article that happened to be adulterated whether he knew it to be such or not. There may be a provision elsewhere in the Bill which modifies the clause but as it stands it looks frightfully drastic.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend will see that clause 17 modifies the one we are discussing. The former reads as follows:
If the person accused proves to the magistrate before whom any prosecution is brought for selling, offering or exposing for sale any article of food or drug that is adulterated or misbranded, that he purchased the article in question for and as an article of the same nature, substance and quality as that demanded of him by the purchaser or inspector, with a written warranty to that effect, and produces the said warranty, or other evidence satisfactory to the magistrate, at the trial, and also prove that he sold it in the same state as that in which he purchased it and that he could not with reasonable diligence have obtained knowledge of its adulteration or misbranding, he shall be discharged from such prosecution

. And so on. So far as the point raised by my hon. friend is concerned, the provision is the same as it has been for many years. In fact, section 17 is designed to make it a little easier for the innocent party than is the case under the existing law. I should think that in practice very few would secure a
fMr. Rowell.1
warranty with the article when they bought it; under the provision as it stands the person accused must not only secure the warranty but must produce it to the justice trying the case. I should think it would be quite sufficient if he established to the satisfaction of the justice that he bought it as of the kind and quality described in the section; and that he should not be required to have procured a warranty at the time he actually purchased it. When we come to section 17, I intend to propose an amendment to this effect.

When is the notice referred to in subsection 1 of section 17 given? If it is given on the day of the hearing, it would then be too late to obviate the expense of prosecution, and I assume that that is the purpose of that part of the section. It seems to me that if a man is absolutely innocent he should not be called ujfon to pay any costs. There should be a provision in the section that if the person accused establishes his innocence at the first sitting of the court he should not be held responsible for the payment of costs incurred by the prosecutor.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The section contemplates not only that the person accused shall give notice of intention to rely upon the defence referred to, but, in subsection 2, that he shall bring before the court the party from whom he purchased the article. The object is that the person who is really responsible shall pay the penalty.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 17-want of knowledge:

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I move to amend section 17 by striking out the following words:
With a written warranty to that effect, and produces the said warranty, or other evidence satisfactory to the magistrate, at the trial.
Then the only obligation resting upon the accused will be to satisfy the magistrate that he purchased the article bona fide in the manner provided in the section and that he could not with reasonable diligence have obtained knowledge of its adulteration, or misbranding; and that he must bring before the court the party from whom he purchased it.

If prosecutions are taken without good reason, it is only fair that the costs should be borne, not by the accused, but by the prosecutor. If the person accused proves to the satisfaction of the magistrate that he has not been guilty of negligence he should not be liable to the payment of costs.

The first day of the hearing is the first opportunity that the defendant has of giving the notice required; and if he does not give it then and proves his innocence, under this clause he is liable for the payment of costs. That should not be so. It should be provided that if the accused brings the matter to the attention of the court at the first hearing and establishes his innocence, he should not be responsible for costs. Of course, if he fails to bring it to the attention of the court at the first hearing, I agree, he should be responsible for the costs, even if the case against him is dismissed.	*

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Reading the latter part of subsection 1 with subsection 2, the net result is that he may give the notice at any time before the case is disposed of and the third party is brought in. My interpretation of it is that he would not be liable to the costs if he gave the notice and brought in the third party at any time before the court disposed of the case.

In view of what the minister has said. I assume that he would not object to adding to the section a provision that the magistrate shall decide also the question of costs. The minister's interpretation may be all right, but the interpretation of the judge might be quite different.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have not the least objection to inserting the words " including the question of costs " after the words "merits of the case," in subsection 2.
iMr. BOYS: As it stands now the provision might lead to serious injustice, although not involving a very large sum. Let us assume that the defendant is in the police court on this first hearing and that, by his own evidence and iby that of his vendor, he establishes to the satisfaction of the magistrate that he is not guilty. The case should then and there be dismissed, but as he has given no previous notice whatever, according to the words in lines 29 and 30, he is liable to pay the costs incurred by the prosecutor. If the case then stood adjourned, not as to him, or even as to him, and came up another day, counsel might well argue that he had given notice on a previous occasion that he would rely on the clause, and the defendant should not be held responsible for the costs. But cases which are ps clear as that will be disposed of at the first hearing and the costs should not be imposed on the defendant. I do not see how subsection 2 affects the matter in any degree
whatever. It gives power to bring in the third party, but the third party is brought in only when it is perfectly manifest that the defendant is not responsible and the case as regards the defendant is at an end. Therefore, something should be inserted to make it clear that if the defendant gives that notice at the first hearing at which he appears he should not have to pay costs, or at all events, there should be a provision that the magistrate should be enabled, even at a later date than the first hearing, to relieve him of costs if he is innocent.
iMr. ROWELL: One of the objects of this olause is undoubtedly to offer some inducement to the man who is being proceeded against to bring in the party really responsible for the wrong, so that the defendant does not become relieved of the costs if he has actually violated the laws unless he does two things; first, unless he gives notice that he intends relying on this defence; second, unless he brings, or takes proceedings to bring before the court the party primarily responsible for committing the wrong. If any accused claims the benefit of this section and applies to have a summons issued to bring before the court the party who, he says, is really responsible for the wrong, the magistrate could not then dispose of the case in the first instance, but would adjourn the hearing until he had all parties before the court and would then deal with it under subsection 2. That would seem to be the logical method of dealing with the case.

That is undesirable, because it simply means bringing all the witnesses back to another sitting of the court and piling on more expense. If an innocent party appears before the court and establishes his innocence, he should not be brought back except as a witness for the prosecution.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Under section 34 of the old Act, which corresponds with subsection 1, the defendant must procure at the time 'he purchases a certificate as to the quality in the form prescribed in the schedule. My hon. friend will see that the olause as now proposed is a greater protection to the innocent man, that is, innocent in the sense that he acted without knowledge.

I would suggest that the words:
Unless he gives notice in court that he will rely on the above defence and calls-

Be substituted for the words:
Unless he has given due potice to him that he will rely on the above defence and has called-
Then, when he is in the court room, his counsel will intimate to the court that he is claiming the provisions of this section and that he has with him or undertakes to call the party from whom he purchased. In that event everybody is protected, and an innocent person cannot be called upon to pay costs or to submit to .a second appearance in court with the consequent expense.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I move that the clause be amended to read:
Unless he has given notice to him or gives notice to the court that he will rely on the above defence and has called or calls the party from whom he purchased the said article into the case as hereinafter provided.

Is there any procedure provided in the Bill for the bringing in of the third party? Third party procedure is well known to the Supreme and County Courts, but it is entirely new, at least I never heard of it, in a magistrate's court.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is provided in subsection (2). So far as the third party is concerned we are not changing the law in any respect from what it has been for many years. It is -quite true, as my hon. friend says, that bringing in a third party is not a common practice in proceedings of this kind, although it is quite common in civil proceedings, but just to meet the class of case we have been discussing this afternoon and evening provision has been made in the Act respecting the adulteration of food and in this Bill for bringing in the person whom the accused declares to be the party from whom he purchased the goods, so that the magistrate may hear all the parties and determine who is responsible. Subsection (2) provides that a summons may issue to bring the third party before a court.

But a magistrate has no power to issue a summons except upon a duly laid information. Who is going to lay the information in this case? A magistrate has no jurisdiction to institute criminal proceedings except upon a duly laid information, and if proceedings are not instituted in that way they will -not stand at all.
Mr'. ROWELL: I appreciate the importance of what my hon. friend has in -mind, but if he iwill look at subsection (2) he will

see that the process as against the third party is initiated upon the sworn declaration of the vendor; that is, the man who is charged with the violation of the law must first make a sworn declaration before the magistrate that he purchased the article in good faith and as provided in subsection (1). Upon that sworn declaration the magistrate issues a summons to a third party calling him -into the case. When the summons issues and the third party is brought in subsection (2) provides the magistrate shall "at the same time hear all the parties and decide upon the entire merits of the case not only as regards the person originally accused, 'but also as regards the third party so brought into the case." I do not think that so far any -trouble has -arisen as to the magistrate's jurisdiction under this section, and it has been the law for a -great many years.
Does the minister say that the Act provides that upon the sworn declaration of the accused the magistrate shall have jurisdiction to issue the summons?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is what I understand the Act to mean. It is not set out in so -many words.

But the magistrate
must have jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think this gives him
jurisdiction. So far as I am aware, his jurisdiction has never been -questioned under this clause and it has been in force a gTeat many years. There i-s nobody else who can issue the summons except the magistrate.

-But -at commo-n law,
and by -all the decisions of courts-the books are full of it-the (magistrate can only issue a process upon a duly laid information. That is the basis of his jurisdiction. He cannot of his own motion institute proceedings. . Suppose a -man refused to come to -court and that -a warrant issues and he is put in gaol. He is brought up under habeas corpus or certiorari and the court would hold that the magistrate had no jurisdiction unless an information of a criminal character has been laid against the man, and the whole thing would go up in smoke.

I think the point raised by my hon. friend is well worthy of the minister's consideration. It seems to me that this is in direct contrast to the practice of the criminal courts. You will observe that the declaration is not in the nature of an

information, 'but i't is the sworn statement of the defendant in the case, given on his own behalf, to clear himself from the charge made against him. Upon that a summons is issued. What would the summons be for? Not to answer a distinct charge laid against the third party. It would be issued in the only case pending, namely, against the defendant who gives this evidence and makes the declaration. It is true that this third party might attend and be put in the witness box, not as a defendant or as a witness in a case against himself, but as a witness in the case against the original defendant, and he might claim the protection of the law and refuse to answer on the ground of incrimination. It seems to me that as against the third party the procedure should be very much the same as in liquor cases. A man charged with being drunk is called upon to state where he got his liquor. He gives that evidence, and then a fresh information is immediately laid against the party from whom he got the liquor, and a fresh case is commenced. I think my bon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) is quite right: 'There should be another information laid against the third party, who should be called, not as a witness, but as a defendant in a case against himself. I do not know what the practice has been in the past so far as this is concerned, but I have had some little experience in criminal law and I never heard of such a thing before. It seems to me it requires careful consideration before such a far-reaching change is made in the existing criminal law .

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I confess I am not quite able to follow the view of my hon. friend on this section. I should think it is quite clear that the third party is not called there as a witness, but as a third party in the case, and that he becomes a party to the proceedings. The procedure is not dissimilar, if one may so state it, to the procedure in civil cases where a third party comes in. In a civil case, if a third party is brought in, he is brought in at the instance of the defendant, who must file his claim over as against the third party. This section provides that he must file a sworn declaration. That declaration must set out that he purchased the goods from this third party, that he purchased them in good faith, that he purchased them as an article of the same nature, substance and quality as that demanded of him by the informant, and that he sold the article in the same state as that in which he purchased it. Therefore, he sets out in the sworn declaration the facts which constitute an offence
under the Act. That declaration, I would submit, would be in substance an information of an offence committed under the terms of the Act. Upon that the magistrate issues a summons, not to bring the third party there as a witness, but, as the section provides, to call such third party into the case." He thereby becomes a party to the proceedings. Then the magistrate "shall at the same time hear all the parties and decide upon , the entire merits of the case, not only as regards the person originally accused, but also as regards the third party so brought into the case." It would be an adjudication just as we have under the third party procedure in civil cases. I shall discuss the matter further with the Department of Justice, and in the meantime let the matter stand.
If a manufacturer in Quebec sold foodstuffs to a retailer in Ontario and the retailer were prosecuted, how could an order of a magistrate in Ontario be enforced against the manufacturer in Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He could be brought before the magistrate in Ontario upon a warrant backed by a magistrate in his own province, as in the case of information laid under the criminal code.
This is not under the criminal code.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is a Dominion statute applicable to all provinces. However, I am prepared to discuss the matter further with the department. I agree that there should be no uncertainty regarding the law in dealing with matters that are criminal or quasi-criminal in character, and if there is ambiguity it should be cleared up.

As I read the section, the
sworn declaration is really in the nature of an information, and it becomes the duty of the defendant to lay that information. If this "sworn declaration" were made "information," the magistrate on the strength of the information could issue a summons and the same end would be attained.

My hon. friend will
find laid down in part 15 of the criminal code the provision that before any magistrate can make any criminal motion against a person there must be information.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I move that section 17
stand.
Motion agreed to: section 17 stands.
On section 18-no Gertiorari.

I hope the minister
will withdraw this section.

Does the minister not think it proper to give the appeal in this case to the divisional courts? In most summary conviction cases there is an appeal, in Ontario at least, to a divisional court. The appeal is heard within two or three weeks of the sitting of the police court, and at a very trifling expense. In view of the fact that the fines imposed in this Act run up to as high as $500 it seems to me that there should be some protection against conviction by a justice of the peace in the country, who very often has not very much experience in matters of this kind.
This seems to be a crude way of getting clear of the defects contained in section 17. The minister provides an absolutely bad procedure in section 17, and then says you cannot review it.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I move that section 18
stand.
Motion agreed to: section 18 stands.
On section 19-voluntary payments.

Will any part of the
amount voluntarily paid under this section be given to the prosecutor?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The amount voluntarily-paid to the minister will be dealt with "as if lawfully recovered upon prosecution," and that I think would permit of a portion of it being paid to the informant. This does not go as far as the old Act, which provided that, upon examination being made, and the sample being found to be adulterated, the minister might exercise his discretion and simply require the party to pay the cost of procuring and analysing the sample, and not proceed further. We have not continued that provision, but have provided for voluntary payment of the fine which would be imposed, the expense of prosecution in court being obviated.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Is there any
section of the Bill which pre-supposes a payment of that kind or makes provision for it?	'

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The old clause provided, as the present Act does, for taking a sample for analysis, the result of such analysis to be communicated to the party. It then goes on to say: '
The Minister may at his discretion cause the result of the analysis to he communicated to the vendor and require him to pay the party specified in the second schedule of this Act for the cost of procuring and analysing said sample. And should such vendor refuse or neglect to do so, the minister may then cause legal proceedings to be taken against him as hereinafter provided.

The only penalty you might impose at the discretion of the minister would be the penalty of paying the cost of procuring and analysing the sample. If he did. not choose to pay that voluntarily a prosecution might be instituted under the Act. It appeared to the officers administering the department that that was not a very satisfactory provision. If a person is to be let off without a prosecution he should pay the penalty which the law provides, but if the party comes forward and is prepared to pay the fine the minister should not be compelled to prosecute him before the court in order to recover it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The old law, under which cases had to come before the courts in-the first instance, would give greater protection to the accused than this law, would it not?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, the old law did not require them to proceed in the manner I have mentioned. An offender might be prosecuted in the first instance, but it gave discretion to the minister to make him pay the cost of procuring and analysing a sample. Under the present Bill the minister may permit him to pay the fine voluntarily without going through any procedure in court.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If the offender pays the penalty under this clause is he still liable to prosecution in court?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

This Is a new departure and I think it is a discretion that the officers of the department would do well to avoid altogether. A man comes to court and pleads guilty; a fine is imposed upon him; and that is the end of it. An officer of the Government can state in court the degree of leniency they want to extend to the offender. But it is rather objectionable that the minister should exercise this power in place of the magistrate.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am quite prepared to
admit that there is a good deal in what my hon. friend has said. I hesitated about the section for the very reason that he has mentioned, but in a case of adulteration the party pays the penalty which the law imposes, and this simply gives power to receive it and deal with it as in a case of conviction. It is for the House to say. I am not disposed to press it. I understand that this is done under the Customs 9 p.m. law and is not a new departure.
A similar law was administered by the Department of Inland Revenue be-

fore, and I am not aware that any difficulty has arisen under it.	[DOT]

There is provision here for a second offence, but if a fine of this kind has been paid to the minister it cannot be regarded as a first conviction and there cannot be a second offence. A second *offence means that a man has been convicted, that he is brought up a second time for the same offence, and the record of the *court shows that he has already been convicted. The fact that a man had paid a fine would not constitute a record of conviction and a man could never be convicted of a second offence under a procedure of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is quite true that it
would not constitute an offence which would lay the basis for a proceeding in a [DOT]second offence. The three penalty sections might stand and I will give them further consideration.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 20-refusal of access:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is that similar to the old law?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, it is practically the same.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The clause is very far-reaching. It would make liable to this penalty any person who had some food or drug in his possession and did not happen to show it when the inspector came. He might have his store full of these commodities, and if he omitted to show every one of them he would be liable.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is necessary to make
it pretty broad to afford full opportunity for inspection.

Why should this clause *pass? With all the inspectors that we shall have in cities, towns and municipalities, a retailer would require to have a man whose *special duty it would be to show the inspector around. All that the inspector requires to do is to procure a sample and have it analysed to see whether the article is adulterated or not. I do not see why an inspector should be shown around and given access to everything in the store. It is practically impossible. This is an imposition; it is not legislation.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is the law as it stands on the statute book now.

Why should not the
words " or omits '* be left out? I understand the purport of the section is that a 62 .
man is guilty of an offence if he in any way obstructs the officer or keeps him from seeing anything that is in the shop. If the inspector is given full access to the shop, why should it be made criminal if the shopkeeper omits to call his attention to something that he has not specially asked to see? Why not leave out the words "or omits"? Those words in the section, which throw the burden upon the shopkeeper to take the inspector around, should be left out. If the shopkeeper affords full opportunity to the inspector to examine everything in the store that is all that should be asked.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The clause in that respect is exactly ^he same as the law that has been in existence fo-r a very long time. No difficulty has arisen in connection with its administration, no charge of any unfairness has been made, and the law having so far worked satisfactorily, I submit we would not be well advised to change it at the present time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Would it not be well to amend the clause so as to make it apply to any person who "knowingly or intentionally omits," btc. That would be a protection and yet would not deprive the provision of any value that it has.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 21-possession of materials by manufacturer usable for adulteration.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is this the same provision as in the old Act?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The principle is the same but the proposed section is somewhat broader. In the case of intoxicating liquors the present section provides that if any ingredients for adulteration are found in the case then the results mentioned follow. The new section makes the iapplieation general both as to food and drink covered by the Act. I will give the committee a concrete illustration of why this section has been broadened. On one occasion the officers of the department went to a certain establishment where, it was suspected, adulteration was taking place. They found a large amount of butter on one side of the room and a large amount of oleomargarine on the other with a mixer in between. What was intended was quite obvious, but not finding the actual adulteration *there was no offence under the law. If parties have adulterants on the premises for which they cannot .satisfactorily account 'then they will be held to be in the business of producing adulterated products. That is the object of [the section.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On section 22-false label or neglect to label.
I 'would like to know whether the provision in the first part of the section applies to the owner or to the servant or to both.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the employee knowingly attaches a misleading label or mark to any article or package of food or drugs, and thus is a party to deceiving the public, he, as well as the owner, is guilty of the offence.
A twelve or thirteen-year old boy, in receipt of three or four dollars a week, who is ordered to do this work, would come under this provision of the section.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I should think that in such a case the boy would not be prosecuted but the owner would. It is not possible to provide for all possible exceptions without weakening the general effect of the law.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This clause contains the word "knowingly" which I suggested might be inserted in the previous clause. My hon. friend from Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) then asked the minister how he would prove "knowingly." I would like to pass the question on to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Let me give an actual case that occurred in the administration of the law, because it shows the purpose of the section. A man was selling a syrup not made of maple syrup but with a device attached showing maple trees with the spiles in them, with the object of making the purchaser think he was buying maple syrup when such was not the case.
Such a case as that should be severely dealt with.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In such a case as mentioned no one could doubt that the device was knowingly attached to the container.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 23-expenses, counsel fees.
The subsection as to fees in this clause should be omitted.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The section in that respect is exactly the same as the existing law. I am free to say that I was surprised when I came across that provision in the law, but it has been the law for a long time. Then, section 47 of the existing law provides for the expenses of prosecution, including the usual counsel fee, in the discretion of the judge. It is also a provision of the present
[Mr. Rowell. 1
law that if a prosecution is dismissed as being instituted" without reasonable and proper cause, the costs of the defence shall be taxed against the prosecutor. If we include the provision regarding counsel fee, I think we should include also this provision for the payment of costs by the prosecutor who is held to have had no just ground for believing that there had been a violation of the law. I therefore move that the following be added to section 23 as subsection (3):
(3) In the case of a private prosecutor, if the prosecution is dismissed as being institued without reasonable and probable cause, the costs of defence shall be taxed against the prosecutor.

Ninety-five per cent of the magistrates in this country have not the slightest conception of what a counsel fee is; yet they are asked to say what shall be a reasonable counsel fee. If the Government engages counsel to prosecute these cases, they themselves ought to pay counsel; that has been the practice all along in every branch of the administration of justice, customs and inland revenue. I certainly did not know that there was such a provision anywhere as this. I hope that the minister will leave counsel fees, briefs and all such things as these to the Superior Courts, where there are competent authorities to deal with them.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If we strike out that provision we add so much more to the expense of enforcing the law. My information is that the counsel fee is almost invariably included by the magistrate, though in some few cases the magistrate may refuse to fix or to include the fee. Generally speaking, a fee of about $20 is what is usually fixed by the magistrate in these contested cases. Most of the parties who are found guilty under the Adulteration Act have substantial means and can afford to pay this cost of administration; we are anxious not to add to the burdens of the public treasury in enforcing the law.

Why not state that the
fee shall be $20, no more and no less? " Reasonable fee " is a somewhat equivocal term.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No complaints have been received against the provisions of the old law, and no difficulties have so far arisen in its administration. Perhaps it would be wiser to leave it as it is.

There are too many of these enactments which enable a magistrate to award costs against the defendant when the prosecution is unsuccessful. I have never

yet seen the case where a defendant who has , had to employ counsel and pay his own witness fees has been able to get any costs awarded against those who brought him there without proper cause. My idea would be to leave the question of counsel fees and costs, except ordinary police court costs, entirely out. But if you make provision concerning them, then if the prosecution is successful let them get costs, and if the defendant is successful let him get costs. Let the costs on both sides be taxable on the same scale.

Where is an offence
under this Act made a criminal offence?
