speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. C. C. Ballantyne (Minister of Marine and Fisheries), Bill No. 21, to amend the Canada Shipping Act (Certificates of Service), was read the second time, and the House went into- committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-requirements for certificates of service as masters and mates:

How many schools for the training of masters and mates are there in Canada, where are they located, and

how many masters and mates passed the requisite examination within the last year? I should like the minister to give us some idea of what is being done in this connection. Is an effort toeing made to get properly qualified masters and mates without taking extreme measures?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have a number of schools throughout Canada, but, I am sorry 'I cannot give the exact number at the moment, nor can I say how many masters and mates have been granted certificates within the past year. I can only repeat what I stated when the resolution was under discussion, that a real shortage of masters and mates for sailing vessels not over 750 tons does exist, and that during the war I had to take the necessary authority under the War Measures Act to remedy the situation. The shortage still exists.

Is it not a fact that in connection with the School of Technology at Halifax there is a branch for the training of masters, mates, engineers and so forth? Has the minister any record of what is being done at that school in this respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. member is quite right, there is a school at Halifax; there are others at Quebec, Kingston, and different centres throughout the country. I have not with me the figures as to the number of masters and mates who have qualified, but the object of this Bill is to supply the shortage.

Is it the intention of the minister that the test or examination shall be conducted by a shipmaster, or by some proper authority apart from the minister himself? If so,' what machinery is provided for the proper examination of masters and mates so that they can obtain the certificate provided for under this proposed legislation?
Mr. 'BALLANTYNE: The man who wishes to become master or mate of a sailing vessel must have served on a sailing ship for twelve months at some time during the past ten years. He has to appear before the examiners of masters and mates, and pass an oral examination on the rules of the road. He must be able to take observations, read signals, and must know all that is required of any one desiring to become certificated either as master or mate. The only difference between this examination and the one for a competency certificate is that in the latter case the man takes a written examination, and in this case the examination is oral. I think my hon. friend will
fMr. McKenzie.]
agree that many excellent men who could not pass a written examination have the necessary training and technical knowledge to pass an oral examination. We are not lowering the standard at all, inasmuch as this is 'limited to sailing vessels not over 750 tons.

The .minister says that among the qualifications required is ability to take observations and ascertain his position at sea, his latitude and longitude, and the amount of leeway his vessel may have made during the night, or in a storm, or from currents. I can find no such provision in the Bill. It does not provide that he shall toe able to work out chronometer time for instance, or be able to work the sextants and locate the position of the ship. If an examination of that kind must be passed, much of my objection to the Bill will vanish, but I can find no such provision here. I think it would be an extraordinary thing for this House solemnly to legislate that a man can take charge of a 750-ton ship with a crew and valuable cargo, who, if he struck a storm or a spell of bad weather, would be absolutely unable to ascertain where he was. If that is the kind of men we are willing to see take charge of our ships, the House must take the responsibility. If the minister says that they must possess this necessary knowledge I should like to see it clearly stated in the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Section 85 provides that the man must produce "satisfactory evidence of his sobriety, experience, ability and general good conduct on board ship; and (c) passes the sight-test and the prescribed examination in signalling." He must also understand signalling and be able to find his position. He must know the rules of the road and everything that a mate or captain would need to know. The examination is along the usual lines. I am only asking that the Shipping Act be brought, not up to date, but from 1870 up to ten years prior to 1920. I can assure my hon. friend that no master or mate will be certificated unless he possesses the necessary navigation knowledge and technical skill.	.

I do not think that any person who has a fair knowledge of the working of a ship and of nautical matters can complain that the requirements to-day are too strict It is not a very difficult matter to pass the examination prescribed. If it is not the purpose of this Bill to make it still easier, and to open the door to men to take charge of ships who could

not take charge of them under the present law, it seems to me it has no purpose at all. I take it for granted that the purpose of this legislation is to lower the qualifications required, and to open the door wide to almost any person to take charge of a ship. A ship of 750 tons is quite a craft, and will have quite a number of men on board. It is not necessarily a schooner, rigged vessel; it may be a square-rigged vessel. The minister will readily understand that there is quite a difference in the working of the two. The handling of a square-rigged vessel, a barque, a barquan-tine, a -brig or brigantine, requires very different handling from a schooner-rigged vessel. The man must know how to set the yards and sails, and send his men aloft on the yards. So far as I can see, this Bill makes no provision for requiring that knowledge before a man can obtain a certificate. Perhaps the minister has in his mind some examination, but I think it is always best and safest for the public to have these things in the Bill when the legislation is being put through the House.
I regret that the minister should take the view that he is bringing this Act up to date by making it possible for a man who served a year on board a vessel ten years ago to obtain a certificate. I have already explained as well as I could why this provision was in the old Act. Formerly a large number of men made their living by going to sea when we had no examinations; and when the Act was passed it was thought hard that such men, although they had no technical education nor hook learning, should be thrown out of employment. Provision was therefore made that if they could show that they had done the work and were able to do it they would be given an opportunity to obtain service certificates. It must be remembered that a servi'ce certificate is different from the certificate which a man gets by virtue of examination, and now that the law has been in force for a number of years any man who contemplates being, a captain should be prepared to comply with that law and give adequate proof of his knowledge. The same justification for service certificates does not exist to-day as existed when the law was first introduced thirty or forty years ago. 1 protest against this proposal, and I have shown the minister that I am not alone in my opposition to it. The Association of Shipmasters of British Columbia, as well as the Association of the Maritime Provinces, through their president at Halifax, have sent me telegrams protesting against this
matter, which I have communicated to the minister. I regret that I do not seem to receive much sympathy in this House in this respect. The shipmaster's profession has always been regarded as an excellent one, but now that profession is to be degraded, and hardly any qualification will be required of a man who wants to take charge of a ship. Any person may command a vessel who has been for a year on board of any sort of craft, no matter of what description; he can come before the minister and obtain a certificate to be the master of a ship of 750 tons; I have already brought to the notice of the minister the fact that certain requirements in -our own Act provide for the approval of the Board of Trade in England before our certificates are of any value. This very question has ' been before Canadian conferences in England, and if the minister will consult an ex-minister who is now a Judge of the Supreme Court he will learn that that gentleman had this question under consideration *vand endeavoured to obtain from the home authorities full power for this Parliament to abrogate the jurisdiction which the British Parliament has over our legislation in regard to shipping, but that power has never been obtained. Nevertheless we are ignoring the jurisdiction of the British Parliament and taking the whole business into our ovn hands. There is nothing in the British Nprth America Act giving us control over shipping. We started out in Confederation with the Shipping Act of 1854, and we also had the British Shipping Act ot 1894 with its amendments practically all of which applies to this coimgy. However, the minister chooses to go on in hio own way and send men across the Atlantic with certificates of the kind to which I have raised such strong objection, and under the British Shipping Act 1 rather think that these men will get themselves into trouble. Many years ago I discussed this matter with Hon. Mr. Brodeur, who was then Minister of Marine and Fisheries and is now a Judge of the Supreme Court, and on his authority I can inform the House that he had this very question under consideration with the British Government. The question is not settled. If the minister elects to ignore this fact and all the other circumstances to which X have alluded he does so on his own responsibility.

I think my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) is putting the case a little too strongly when he says that any man who goes to sea for a year is allowed,

under this Act, to take charge of a ship. I do not understand the Act in this way. The Act provides that any man who has acted as master of a ship for a year will be qualified, which is very different from the interpretation of my hon. friend. He must have become a master by some means or other, possibly by permission of the department; but it is necessary that he shall have had one year's experience as a master before he can be qualified. This is a certain amount of experience and ought to weigh with the department. I have not much sympathy with the idea that we should be controlled in our shipping laws by the dictates of Downing street. This is purely a domestic matter., We are discussing the qualifications of captains on Canadian ships belonging to Canadian citizens and registered in Canadian ports, and I do not thnk that the home government should have anything at all to do with such an exclusively- Canadian matter. There are certain questions in regard to shipping that refer to the trade of the Empire, matters in which the Board of Trade in England is interested. One case that occurs to my mind just now is the deckload law. I was in the House some years ago when an attempt was made to change the law in regard to deckloads in the lumber trade. The old law permitted a ship to load with, I think, three feet of deckload. The ships after this law was passed were built to contain two decks, and the construction of the law was that this three feet was on the lower deck, so that the shipowner had to leave the rest of the lower deck empty. It was a hardship for Canadian shipowners and merchants shipping lumber, and it took some years to get the matter adjusted. The Board of Trade in England claimed that they had some interest in the matter and that it conflicted with the terms of the Merchants Shipping Act, but then finally gave their consent to an amendment of the law, so that the three feet of deckload could be put on the top deck and not on the second. I do not think we ought to ask the British Government anything about a question of this kind. This is a Canadian question pure and simple. I quite agree with my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) that men ought to be encouraged to pass examinations.
I would like to see a captain carrying his regular certificate issued by a Canadian board or by the Minister of Marine. That would be an ideal system. But captains are very scarce at the present time on the coasts of Canada and it is with great diffi-

culty that captains are found to man the ships we have. Ships have increased largely during the war but the same increase did not take place in the number of certificated men. No later than this morning I received a telegram from a gentleman who has built a ship of 300 or 400 tons in my constituency and who is in trouble about a captain; it is impossible for him to get a captain to take that ship to sea. The ship is ready. He has a competent man who has had twenty years experience as the master of a small vessel -a vessel so small that he did not need under our laws to take out a certificate,; consequently he has not the necessary certificate to take charge of this larger vessel. Yet, he is a good enough man, the owner knows he is good enough, and the people who are insuring the ship are quite satisfied with him. Why should he not be allowed to take that vessel to sea? The owner ought to be the best judge as to his competency. I do not think that the danger to the crew amounts to very much in the case of a man who has had that much experience and who is a careful seaman.
My hon. friend knows as well as I do that for many years we did not have certificates at all in Nova Scotia, yet we built up a great mercantile fleet prior to Confederation and something was done in that direction after Confederation. It was experience we trusted and it worked out very well. There is a great deal to be said in favour of that system. The United States came to that conclusion many years ago. They had the same experience and the same development as we have had here. A large number of coasting vessels were built on the coasts of the United States., Seamen were scarce and the Government of the United States, a good many years -ago, made a law similar to the one which my hon. friend is -now trying to pass providing that ships of less than 700 tons did not require to have -certificated captains. That is the law at present in the United States, and it is with the United States that we are competing. There is much to be said in favour of the Bill. I feel inclined to vote for it. I do not see the same danger from it that my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) seems to see. I think the Bill will be found to be very useful to the trade on the coasts of eastern Canada at all events and I do not think there is very much danger in taking this step, especially as it has already been taken in the United States and our ships in business in South America and the West Indies have to compete with the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In answer to the
hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), I would say again that no master or mate can get a certificate simply by reason of having served twelve months on ,a sailing ship during the last ten years. All have to serve for twelve months and if a man wishes to become the master of a sailing ship not larger than 750 tons he has to appear before an examining hoard of masters and mates and pass an examination which is much more rigid than that prior to 1870. Prior to 1870, they did not call upon a man who desired to be a master or mate to go through the eye or signalling test. A man can only obtain a service certificate as a captain or a mate if he passes the rigid examination which is prescribed.
I find in the memorandum which is before me now that the Masters and Mates Act has always provided for the issuing of service certificates to masters and mates. Under sections 95, 96 and 97 of the Canada Shipping Act a master or mate is properly certificated if he holds a service certificate. Under this Act upwards of 4,800 masters' and mates' certificates have been issued. With all due deference to one of my predecessors, Hon. Mr. Brodeur, I am sorry that I cannot agree with him. With regard to a man holding a masters certificate and going to ,a United Kingdom port on a vessel not over 750 tons, the master of a Canadian registered vessel is granted clearance from a port of the United Kingdom if he holds a service certificate just the same as if he held a competency certificate. There will be no trouble about a Canadian captain holding a service certificate clearing from any United Kingdom port. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has pointed out quite truly that our American friends do not ask for any certificates whatever for a master or mate on a sailing ship up to 750 tons. We have to compete with our neighbours to the south and as we are much more careful than they are, for our men have to pass the examination that I have referred to besides sailing for twelve months on a sailing ship; whereas, across the line a man can go abroad one of these vessels as master without any service at all. The British Board of Trade issue masters 'service certificates without examination to certain officers of the Royal Navy. I think that this House is quite within its rights in granting these certificates to men who have the necessary knowledge and pass the necessary oral examination.

If the minister is right that we can branch out for ourselves entirely and make our own navigation laws without any reference to the rules of the road or to British jurisdiction, why not do it? Why not introduce an Act and dispense entirely with any knowledge of the rules
10 p.m. of the road? We cannot, and why not? We cannot do it because of the conference of the maritime countries of the world which have agreed to the rules of the road. These rules of the road are binding on the British Empire of which we are a part and we cannot change them. That is the law that guides us and we cannot change one letter of it. The minister says in one breath that we are absolutely independent of the British marine law and in the next that we must comply with it. He puts in here a provision with reference to the rules of the road. What rules of the road? We have no rules. If we do not come within the British rules of the road and within the British Act we cannot sail ships. We have only one flag. The Canadian flag is not recognized as a shipping flag. Every Canadian ship, no matter where it goes, must have the British flag, there is no other flag of ours that is recognized.
I have received from Vancouver a telegram which it is my duty to read. It is dated 22nd March, is addressed to myself, and is as follows;
We strongly endorse your stand and support statements attributed to you on Bill proposing inferior certificates Canadian masters and mates.
Canadian Merchant Service Guild.
I have also received a message from Halifax to the following effect:
Representing the certificated masters and mates of Maritime Provinces strongly protest against Bill granting certificates master and mate sail ships seven hundred fifty tons without duly qualifying. Canadian seagoing certificates recognized in all British ships and possessions. Therefore must equal standard British Board of Trade. Coastwise and lower grades accessible to any man capable of having charge of life and property and standard low enough. Bill gross injustice and should be thrown out or hoisted. If passed will ruin the profession. Shortage of masters exaggerated, and if any primarily due to acting present Government granting permits.
A. W. Innis, President, Shipmasters' Association.
We have1 only two ocean fronts in this country, one on the Pacific and the other on the Atlantic. On both ocean fronts they have a Masters' Association, and both of these associations protest against this legislation as degrading their profession. All I can do is to bring these communications to the attention of the minister; but if he hap-

pens to have some influence brought to bear upon him by people who have ships and who care nothing for the crew of the vessels, care nothing for anything except to make dollars for themselves, and care *not whether their masters are qualified or not-if he is influenced by such men, the responsibility is his. That is not my language, that is the language of the Halifax Board, who say that if any person wants to look properly for ia 'qualified master and will give him a proper wage, they can get him, 'but they cannot secure a first-class master for second-rate pay. The minister seems to be very strong in his conception of the law. I would like him, however, to explain to the Committee and to the country generally the meaning of section 95 of our present Shipping Act, which is chapter 13 of the Revised Statutes, volume 3. As I read that Act, it requires that our legislation shall be approved by the home Government. If that is correct, I still *stand by my position that the certificate which we grant-unless the King in Council of Great Britain approves it under the terms of the Shipping Act of 1894-has no effect at all. If this section of our own Act means anything else, I would like the minister to explain it.

I do not wish to discuss with the hon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie) any point of law, but I notice that in the telegram which he read from Captain Innis that officer does not agree with the hon. gentleman's interpretation of Clause 95 of the Canada Shipping Act. You may have noticed, Sir, that part of that telegram said that Canadian certificates were 'acknowledged all over the world, practically admitting they were as good as any other certificate. Therefore, the hon. gentleman and the President of the Ship Masters' Association of Nova Scotia are not in agreement as to the meaning of Clause 95 of the Canadian Shipping Act.
My reading of the law is that there are three kinds of certificates which can be issued under Clause 95. For example paragraph (a):
Of competency or service for seagoing ships appropriate to their several stations in such ship, or of a higher grade from the minister;
That is to say, if I read the subsection correctly, that the Minister of Marine can issue a certificate of competency of service without any reference whatever to the British Board of Trade or the British 'Government.
Now paragraph (b):

Of competency or service for seagoing ships, appropriate *to their several stations in such ship, or of a higher grade, from the Board of Trade in the United Kingdom.
That is to say, if I understand the wording of the paragraph, that the Minister of Marine can issue a certificate of competency and it is sent to the Board of Trade in England for confirmation or approval. Therefore, I think, under this Act the minister is perfectly within his rights in issuing certificates of competency with, respect to seagoing ships in this country without consulting the Board of Trade or the Government in England.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie) also said that at a conference held some time ago of the different nations, rules of the road were agreed on, and consequently we can have nothing to do with the matter. The reason rules of the road were agreed upon by the different nations was, for example, this:	A French ship coming into
the St. Lawrence river might meet a British or a 'German ship going out, and it would be necessary for the two ships to know the , rules of the road. That is the reason why the rules of the road are international. It has nothing at all to do with the issuance of certificates to masters and mates, and does not affect our position as to whether we can issue the certificates in 'Canada or not.
I might also say that the British Board of Trade are not as particular as they were a few years ago. They are waking up to to the fact that it is not necessary for a man to have a certificate to sail a ship. A few years ago when Canadian ships, or ships from any other nation, went to Great Britain, the British customs officer would not clear them unless they had a certificated master. I have known a number of cases where a ship from the British Domin- * ions that went into Liverpool or Cardiff, or other ports, had to get an English master to clear the ship, and they put him ashore when the pilot went off the boat.
Last summer a number of masters who' were not Certificated had charge of Canadian ships which cleared from Canadian ports, and in my opinion these masters were just as good as the certificated men. They took the ships to England, and the British authorities cleared the ships back with the same men on board without even asking them if they had a certificate. The British-Board of Trade, therefore, realize that it is not necessary in all cases that these men have certificates. I am just as anxious as the member for North Cape Breton and' Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) that masters and

mates who have charge of our ships should 'have" certificates. I should be the last to suggest that we should not endeavour where-ever possible to make our men get certificates. But I do say that under present regulations it is practically impossible for an ordinary man to pass the examination.
I was pleased to hear the member for North Cape Breton refer to the calling of the seamen as a "profession." I will certainly pass that word around when I get home; I will tell my seafaring friends that they are now in a class with lawyers, doctors, clergymen and men of other professions; and they will he proud indeed to hear it.
How about the officers?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. May I ask
the hon. member whether the poem which he proposes to read has any reference to the Bill under consideration?
I think it has.
Is it a poem of the sea?
Yes.

Then it has reference
to this Bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am very sorry, but I have to rule that the hon. member may not read the poem.
It is worth reading, Mr. Chairman. I would like you to hear it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This is not the time or the place to read it. Shall the clause carry?

Well, if I may not read the poetry I shall have to proceed in prose. My idea is that these gentlemen who compose the Halifax Shipmasters' Association need not stay ashore and send telegrams to Ottawa. If they are capable men and want ships, the owners in Nova Scotia will give them ships. If ithey stay ashore, it is their own fault.

The member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) read telegrams from British Columbia, Halifax and Prince Edward Island. It seems strange that these people should send these telegrams; they are well organized and are affiliated with national and international organizations. While in the province of Quebec during the Easter recess I .met quite a few masters and mates who are also members of said organization, and they expressed themselves as willing to submit to the examination. If the masters and mates from other districts were opposed to this measure, I should think that the masters and mates from Quebec would also be opposed to it, but they are not. It seems to me that instead of lessening the efficiency of navigation, this measure would increase it. On the last day of the last session I opposed a Bill which had been introduced dealing with this subject on the ground that a man who was not certificated could take charge of a ship, even if he did not know the rules of the road. This Bill is quite different, it calls for efficiency; and I fail to see why it should not pass. In 1906, the Quebec pilots willingly submitted to an examination, and they are submitting to an annual examination for eyesight, hearing and so forth. If the masters and mates are not competent; if they are not holding certificates, what has happened in years past will happen in years to come. When an accident happens, an inquest is held, and, as has happened on different occasions, the captain or master in charge of the vessel who is responsible for the accident, will not be blamed because nothing can be done to him as he does not hold a certificate, but the pilot who is certificated will have to bear the burden. Therefore, I fail to see why this Bill is not a good one, and I believe it will assist in the securing of competent service. Sub-clause (c) states:
Passes the sight test and the prescribed examination in signalling.
I would suggest that after the word " signalling '' the words " and the rules of the road " be added. I believe these men
[The Chairman.]
should know the rules of the road as well as be able to pass the other tests. *

I have repeatedly
asked the minister to give the committee some explanation as to what is meant by the clause in our old lawn I can understand the minister and his supporters ignoring the British law and saying:	We have
nothing to do with the British law and it has nothing to do with us; the shipping law in Great Britain is no good; we shall turn and have truck and trade with the Yankees. That is what we are going to do; -we are going to accept their laws; we are going to lower the standard of the good old Mother Country who has been the pride of the sea for a thousand years. We are going lio wipe that out and take the regulations under which a few old craft are sent out from Caplin and Gloucester as the standard of our shipping in Canada henceforth. Crystallized, that is the sum and substance of the logic of hon. gentlemen who are supporting this Bill. The minister refuses to give me any explanation of his understanding of sections 95 and 96. It is quite true that he changes two sections of the law which qualify his men; he makes it simple and easy for them to become masters. Has the minister ever come across a man to whom he would offer a certificate of competency in any walk of life and the man would say: I will not take it; I am going to school in order to qualify myself, and I will get the certificate according to law?
I would think the man would be likely to take the certificate at once and take chances on making good. That is the doctrine the minister has established and is supporting here. He is saying to the men of this country: You need not go to school; you need not know anything about navigation; you need not qualify yourself as a first-class seaman, the pride of the British Empire; I will give you a parchment which is good enough. I should like the minister to explain whence the call for this change came. Did the Board of Trade of Quebec, or of Montreal, or of Halifax, or of Sydney, or "of Vancouver, petition the Government asking for this change in the law? If there are such petitions, they should be laid on the Table or put upon Hansard so that we would have that information. So far the minister has not given one word of testimony from any of those institutions which I have mentioned, nor from any other body of men interested in navigation and trade in this country. If there are such demands, I should be disposed to think I am wrong in taking the position I take. The minister may provide a man with a certificate, but when he comes to sending him to sea he will find that section 95 of the Canada Shipping Act stands in the way. That section provides that:
No ship registered in Canada, over one hundred tons registered tonnage, shall go to sea from any port or place in Canada on any voyage not being a coasting voyage, unless the master and first mate or only mate thereof have obtained and possess valid' certificates either,-
(a)	of competency or service for sea-going ships, appropriate to their several stations in such ship, or of a higher grade, from the minister; or,
(b)	of competency or service for sea-going ships, appropriate to their several stations in such ship, or of a higher grade, from the Board of Trade in the United Kingdom; or
(c)	of competency appropriate to their several stations in such ship, or of a higher grade, granted in any British possession-
Here is the part of the Act which the distinguished marine lawyer who now happens to be at the head of the department ignores entirely. He thinks no attention should be paid to the opinion of a Supreme Court judge who says this law is absolutely wrong; he knows better. It is simply an extension of his doctrine about shipmasters; it is not necessary for them to know anything, he thinks, and so why should it be necessary for a lawyer to have any training? He says: I never had any training as a lawyer but I put my opinion above that of even a Supreme Court judge. A knowledge of the law is all nonsense-that is the position he takes. Section 95 provides that, in addition

to the qualifications I have just quoted, there must be added a certificate:
(c) of competency appropriate to their several stations in such ship, or of a higher grade, granted in any British possession, and declared by order of His Majesty in Council, published in the London Gazette, under the provisions of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1894, or of any Act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom containing such provisions, to be of the same force as certificates of competency for foreign sea-going ships granted under the Acts of the Parliament of the United Kingdom relating to merchant shipping.
* To get a certificate in the United Kingdom certain requirements have to be met, certain knowledge must be possessed by the candidate, and an examination must be passed. The minister says:	I will issue
certificates which do not come up to the British standard at all; my requirements will be lower, but at the same time I shall expect the Board of Trade and His Majesty in Council to say that they are of just as high a standard as the certificates issued in Great Britain. If the minister can get His Majesty in Council to do so, that is another matter, but from my knowledge of how things are done in Great Britain I would think that the first thing His Majesty's advisers would do would be to ascertain what are the qualifications required under this new Act and compare them with the qualifications required under the British Act, and then they would advise His Majesty not to give his assent to a proposal that would be a deception upon the face of it. The qualifications required would not be the same.
That is all I care to say about the matter. I still stand by the position I took before, that in education as well as in other matters, we should be advancing not retrograding in this country. The minister will find when he puts his policy before the people and they see that he is undermining ambition and is taking away from young men the desire to qualify for positions in this walk of life, and that in this he has made a mistake. We have a navigation school in my own town, and I know of no one who tried examinations from that school who did not pass; but what encouragement have they to try and qualify themselves now when masters and mates are to be turned out by the minister by the yard, just as if he was measuring off pieces of cloth, without any educational requirements at all?

speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Bill reported.
'Mr. McKenzie.]

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. J. D. Reid, Bill No. 22, .to confirm an Agreement between His Majesty the King and the Corporation of the City of Ottawa was read a second time and the House went into Committee thereon. Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-agreement confirmed:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
The minister
in speaking to the resolution went pretty fully, .1 think, into the main features of the agreement, but there was some information he was to give, when the Bill got into committee, relating to the extent of the increased service the city was rendering the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
The Government have been taking over a lot of property in Ottawa during the last few years, and that means that the city has lost the taxes on those properties. That is one reason why we think there should be an increase in the amount paid to the city. Furthermore, the city are sprinkling water along Wellington street and in front of the Government buildings, and they furnish fire protection to any buildings owned or occupied by the Government. The city also sprinkles the parks and driveways that are maintained by the Ottawa Improvement Commission. All these things represent increased service. The $15,000 that was formerly paid was simply for. fire protection alone. The city's claim, I think, is a very good one, because in the last few years we have been taking over a great deal of property on which the city have been collecting taxes. It is not really an increase that we are giving the city in view of the increased service they are rendering.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: Is it the intention of the Government, when they take over property belonging to other cities, Montreal, for instance, to compensate the city for the taxes they lost?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
No, we have not been doing that. Ottawa is the seat of Government.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY:	The Government
does not pay any taxes on property it acquires in the city of Montreal. *

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
This is the seat of
Government, and the buildings taken over are controlled by the Government.

Mr. DuTREMBLAY: If this principle applies in Ottawa, should it not apply in other cities?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: In that case we should have to adopt a general policy.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
What part of this
agreement provides for the payment by the Dominion of Canada of taxes, or their equivalent, to the city of Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
The Government does
not pay taxes.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: The minister says that the Government pays something in lieu of taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: The city in urging its claim for an increase put up the argument that the fire protection which it afforded the buildings of the Government necessitated a larger equipment.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
Is there anything to
show that the Government recognized that as a sound reason for increasing the allowance to the city? It must_ be recognized as a good argument if the Government is increasing the amount paid to the city.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
The city claims that
they are losing a lot of money by reason of our taking over certain properties. They say that the taxes on the Government property in the city of Ottawa would amount to $483,887. We are not- settling for that, but we are allowing for fire protection, sprinkling of the streets and the use of sewerage, which is an important item. The city also estimated that the tax on civil servants would amount to about $60,000. Taking everything into consideration, the sub-committee that discussed the matter with the city council felt that the amount we are now allowing was reasonable.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
We are to pay more
now than before the civil servants became assessable?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: We paid $15,000 a year, and the civil servants were exempt from income taxation by the city. Now we are paying $75,000, and the civil servants, like any other citizens, will be assessable.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
Now that the civil
servants are being subjected to assessment it must mean a large income to the city of Ottawa. I am not objecting to this at all because a civil servant should pay his way like any other citizen. But we got along with a payment of $15,000 formerly, when civil servants were not contributing anything, and now that they are going to contribute to the income of the city we are raising the city's allowance to $75,000. I do not understand such business, nor can I see any reason whatever for it. We must have been robbing the city to a large extent in former years if it now appears to be necessary that we should increase their allowances by such a large amount. I think the committee requires the fullest possible explanation for this increase from $15,000 to $75,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: The city claimed that $15,000 was not by any means commensurate with the value of the services they rendered the Government, and I think myself that the Government were not paying adequately for those services. The fact of the 'Government having the use of the sewers was a matter of gieat consideration. We would have had to build sewers for all Government property, and the interest on that would amount to a large sum; and we would of course have to have our own fire protection equipment, with men to look after that property and be ready in case of fire,, which would be an annual charge. Again, we would have to keep the streets in front of our own property properly watered. Taking everything into consideration we considered that the city was certainly losing a large amount of money annually, when it was paid only $15,000. As regards the civil servants, it was arranged many years ago that they should be exempt from income taxation, but we could see no reason why the Government should assume that liability in the city of Ottawa and not elsewhere. Civil servants in Ottawa should be put on the same basis as those in any other part of the Dominion so far as income taxation is concerned. I admit that the increase is a large one, but for many months the city refused to accept even it, and it was only latterly that they came to the conclusion that they would accept it for a term of five years. We thought that it should be for a term of ten years, but eventually we compromised and decided on five years. I do not know that in the increased amount the Government will be paying too much for the services which are rendered by the city.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: I think the minister should point out that the Government is also increasing the grant to the Improvement Commission from $60,000 to $150,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: It was $100,000 and we are increasing it to $150,000.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: The Government are getting into the habit of wobbling on this question of the taxation of Dominion Government property. There are two positions to take. One is that we will pay taxes on our property throughout the Dominion and the other is that we will not pay any taxes on Dominion Government property to municipalities. We must live up to one or other of these positions. If we are going to pay the city of Ottawa something in lieu of taxation because it furnishes water and provides sewers, that must also apply to the town in which I live where the public buildings are also provided with drainage, fire protection, and other services. The same principle will apply to every town in Canada. The minister made a big mistake when he capitulated to some of the towns in Ontario in regard to the Grand Trunk. It has brought him trouble already. It has brought him an application from Halifax for a similar concession, and it will bring him applications from all over the Dominion. The country has always proceeded upon the basis that no taxation would be paid and it was so understood whenever a town or city got an expenditure made upon a public building. These public buildings are erected at vast expense to the Dominion, the people are glad to get them, and they have always been glad, until a very recent time, to free them from taxation. Now we are drifting in the wrong direction unless we intend to take the question up boldly and pay taxes all over the Dominion. I do not like to hear the minister say that he is giving this money in lieu of taxes because there are services such as fire protection and sewers provided by the city of Ottawa.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: I understood the hon. gentleman to say that there is an advance of $100,000 and that we get nothing for it.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: Nothing but what we had before.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: Before, we were paying $100,000 to the Improvement Commission, and that amount was expended in beautifying and improving the city of Ottawa, the capital of the Dominion. Fifty thousand dollars of the amount that is being paid is for the Improvement Commission, making $150,000 to be devoted to that work; so that we are getting this increased expenditure for the purpose of beautifying the capital city. I think every hon. member will agree that the capital of the Dominion should Ibe made as attractive as the capital of any other country. The hon. gentleman has asked: "What would the city of Ottawa be without the Parliament buildings"? The Mayor of Ottawa asks: "What would Parliament be without the city of Ottawa "? If we had not the city of Ottawa to make all these expenditures, would we not have to expend a large amount on sewers, waterworks, fire protection, hospitals for our employees, schools, street watering and police protection.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: You have the Dominion Police?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: That is around our own buildings. There are large expenditures that the Government would otherwise have to make. Taking all these things into consideration I do not think the amount is unreasonable. When the discussion commenced, they wanted $80,000 and that did not take into consideration the Improvement Commission at all. We have cut that down to $75,000 and we are allowing $150,000 for improving the city which, I think hon. members will agree, is a good expenditure to be made in the capital.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: Has the minister a statement of the assessed value of the Government property and the tax rate in the city of Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: The taxable real estate in Ottawa was assessed in 1918, for taxation 1919, at $98,983,599.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
Is that Government
property?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
That is the assessment
on the whole of the property in the city of Ottawa. The Government occupies real estate in Ottawa valued, after deducting the value of local Government institutions, at $21,158,190. The Government leases and occupies in addition premises assessed at $4,025,749, and therefore owns, or occupies on lease, about one-fifth of the real estate of the city.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: Did the minister mention the amount the city estimates it lost through the exemption of civil servants from taxation on their incomes?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: I mentioned an amount in the neighbourhood of $60,000. When the City Council made their claim they estimated the amount at $57,175.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
That makes
a total increase of about $170,000 over what was formerly given.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. MeKENZIE: Very valuable property in the city is rented by the Government, and I presume the owners of the property pay the taxes. The few buildings that the country owns in Ottawa should be exempt from taxation. In Halifax, which is not nearly as large as this city, there is far more Government property than there is in Ottawa. The amount of Government-owned property in Halifax, comprising the Fortifications and all the military works in the harbour, is immense, but not a cent of taxes is being paid on that property
either to the city of Halifax or to the province of Nova Scotia. Taxes are being paid to the municipality of Ottawa upon Government property, but nobody from Halifax is asking for the payment of any taxes as far as I know.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
There was a deputation here lately asking for the payment of taxes, and they are hoping, that their demands will be met.
Mr. MeKENZIE: I am not making any argument with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) about what may take place; the Lord only knows what may transpire with this Government, but so far no taxes have been paid to the city of Halifax although there are thousands of dollars' worth of Government property in that city to every thousand dollars' worth of Government-owned property in Ottawa. How can the Government reconcile its payment of taxes to the city of Ottawa when it has not paid a dollar to the city of Halifax? The Government have given out to the world that they are going to pay taxes on the Grand Trunk and Canadian National railway properties, and I suppose when the news went down to Halifax the municipal corporation there said: If the Government are getting so generous as to undertake to pay taxes everywhere, why should they not do so here? I really do not know how the Government can answer the city of Halifax and decline to pay taxes upon the millions of dollars' worth of property they own there while at the same time quite willing to pay taxes in Ottawa and also upon the Grand Trunk and other railway property. I think the principle should be adhered to that Crown property is not taxable.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: We are not giving this grant in the way of taxes. In the capitals of other countries, notably the United States, grants are made almost equivalent to what the Government's taxes would be in return for the benefits they enjoy, as well as towards improving the city. We get the benefits from the municipal corporation I have mentioned and the amount that we are paying, $75,000, certainly is not any too much. I would not like it to go out to the country that what we are paying is by way of taxeA The hon. gentleman has mentioned the Grand Trunk and the Canadian National railways. These lines have been operated by private companies and should continue to pay taxes when they are operated in competition with companies of that class.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
There is no
date mentioned in the schedule, it is left blank. What is the reason of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: I was going to move to amend the agreement so that the date should be the 30th day of March, 1920, and adopt the same date in the schedule.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
Are we to
understand that the minister has already signed this agreement? If this is a concluded contract, what is the object of submitting the matter to Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: Yes, I have signed the agreement, but I cannot pay out the money until it is voted by Parliament.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: There appears to be no clause in the contract which recognizes Parliment one way or the other. The minister should have inserted some provision making the agreement subject to approval by Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
The deputy minister
tells me there is such a provision in the agreement. Yes, I notice it reads that payment is to be made quarterly when due "as soon as may be after the passing of the Act confirming this agreement."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: It is in the first clause of the agreement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
That has
reference to the payment of the $75,000.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext:
Does not the depart-men pay for water supplied to public buildings in other places?
Mr. J. D.'REID: Yes, in accordance with local rates.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: But not taxes?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CORPORATION OP OTTAWA.
speechtext: No.

speechtext:
Schedule agreed to.
Bill reported.
